title: Cover Letter in Full Glory
text:
Carlos Galindo Escajeda · cgalindito@gmail.com · London, UK · +44 (0) 737-677-1146 Eligible to work in the UK
Dear Recruitment Team,
NEF’s A Modern System for Fair Rents set me reading, then mulling, then following one idea into the next — and that is the honest origin of this application for the Social Policy Economist / Quantitative Researcher position. I did not begin with a grand design, least of all a plan to “correct” NEF. It was closer to self-discovery under a hard time limit: the questions I kept pulling on organically coalesced into five linked papers, and the deeper I dug, the more independent lines of inquiry converged — not on whether to intervene in the UK private rented sector, but on a single genuinely contentious question that I did not go looking for: the durability of the intervention, and how far the case for an emergency brake actually extends toward a permanent fair-rents regime. What follows is who built that, how, and the spirit in which I would want to do it from inside your team.
I have worked this way since long before AI existed — starting from scratch, in unfamiliar territory, into the unknown, and against the clock — and I have real confidence that my ingenuity, curiosity, and diligence will get me there on any such occasion. My first serious research ran exactly this pattern. I was working on poverty and demographic risk in a context very different from the UK — Mexico’s low-income household sector — but the policy question was structurally similar to what NEF works on: how do we distribute the burden and benefit of social risk across the income distribution?
That puzzle led me to microsimulate poverty-reduction policy, and doing it meant teaching myself three unfamiliar things at once, from a standing start: how relational databases actually work, well outside the clean tabular data of an econometrics course; how to handle the complex sampling design and processing gymnastics of SEDESOL’s household survey microdata, until I could manipulate and explain it fluidly; and how the Ravallion microsimulation literature operated — estimating a household consumption model, then simulating a policy change to measure how much it shifts each subgroup’s probability of being poor. I learned to program in STATA for that work specifically, and did all of it in under six months — while finishing a master’s thesis on an entirely separate subject: a two-sector overlapping-generations model of household heterogeneity, growth, and convergence between rich and poor. That poverty work became peer-reviewed publications on poverty measurement and policy simulation.
Then I did the part I am proudest of: I packaged the hard-won processing knowledge and gave it away — more than 700 hours of STATA training so that undergraduates could finally mine survey microdata that had gone under-exploited precisely because it was so hard to process, feeding a stream of undergraduate theses. Multiplying the people around me, not only shipping my own output, is the disposition I would bring to your team.
From there I spent the better part of a decade building quantitative models in macro-finance — emerging-market forecasting, Bayesian time-series and DSGE work, even reverse-engineering parts of the Federal Reserve’s FRB/US model to surface scenarios the consensus had missed — at Deutsche Bank, Bank of America, and a global macro fund. Applying to your social-policy team is, for me, a deliberate return to where I began, now with a macro modeller’s toolkit behind it.
So I would ask you to read my recent arrival in UK housing policy the right way. Until I saw this posting I was a tourist in it — but “tourist” is how nearly every one of my best projects has begun; it names how I work, not a ceiling on where I reach. Two honest caveats follow.
First: do not mistake my theoretical papers for a desire to live in abstraction. I am driven to transform material reality — that is what drew me to policy in the first place. But theory and empirics are complements, not substitutes: theory disciplines what we ask, empirics answers it, and the two together correct each other.
You will find these papers are about hardening the welfare case for policies NEF already advocates, grounding them in structural arguments that survive hostile scrutiny. I am not here to replace your policy expertise but to arm it with a particular rigour. The arguments that decide housing policy are fought in public against economists trained in the orthodoxy and trusted by government — and they are won on that ground, with those tools. I can argue there: Breaking the Benchmark uses a mainstream second-best result to take apart the standard case against rent control. That is not the only thing I bring, but it is the hardest to find.
I have laid all this out in the Manifesto — what the five papers are actually for, why each contributes to a specific policy intervention rather than the academic literature, and why theory and action are never in tension in this work.
Second: do not expect me to recite every line flawlessly across an interview table. Across work this broad and this deep, recall matters less than whether it holds up on the page. What matters is that the work is verifiable, genuinely original, and non-trivial by orders of magnitude — not a repackaging of the familiar. I can rebuild any part of it on request, and that ability to reconstruct from first principles, rather than to recite, is the real capability I bring.
A brief note on method. Every load-bearing claim in these papers is verified against a primary source, survives adversarial challenge, or is flagged open — the discipline I work by. The best evidence that this is real and not rhetorical is the fifth paper, A Progressing Problemshift: it applies mainstream philosophy-of-science standards to my own programme and, against my own immediate advantage, downgrades the strongest-looking verdict from “empirically progressive” to “empirically progressing” because the discriminating test is named but still unrun. That is the reflex I would bring under external scrutiny: ambitious claims, strict boundaries, and transparent uncertainty where evidence has not yet closed the question.
The papers map directly onto your specification.
Empirical rigour on large UK datasets. Fiscal Capture in the UK Private Rented Sector is independent, critical panel-data work: a difference-in-differences design across 290 English local authorities (2019–2024), exploiting the April 2020 LHA uplift and April 2021 re-freeze as directionally opposite policy events. Across more than twenty specifications the signature is consistent with landlord capture, with zero sign reversals — and I report the headline coefficient as a deliberate conservative lower bound, naming the attenuation channels (downward nominal rigidity, tenant lock-in) rather than inflating it.
Challenging orthodoxy without overreach. Breaking the Benchmark dismantles the “price controls choke off supply” veto by modelling the UK PRS as a structurally distorted quadruple-object market — shelter, capitalised asset, credit collateral, and fiscal conduit at once. Lipsey–Lancaster second-best logic then cuts symmetrically: once competitive conditions are absent, deregulation forfeits its automatic-efficiency claim exactly as much as regulation does. The paper defends your emergency brake and hardens it — no vacancy decontrol, plus pre-committed statutory exit criteria (sustained ~300,000 net completions and a bottom-quintile cost-burden threshold) that bind the policy to objective milestones rather than open-ended discretion.
A welfare foundation aligned with your mission. Building on the materialist value theory Julio Huato develops in his book and in our co-authored paper, Labor Power as Numéraire, I derived a companion — Rent as Reproduction Cost — that grounds the argument in the physical reproduction of the working population rather than subjective utility. It reframes high rents as a deduction from households’ capacity to sustain and form themselves across generations, turning a CPI-anchored cap from an affordability patch into a structural correction with a coherent welfare rationale.
The five abstracts — one for each paper — are collected in the Research Portfolio. If you only wanted the fastest route through the research, I would suggest starting with Breaking the Benchmark, then Fiscal Capture, then Rent as Reproduction Cost. Nothing in this letter depends on your opening them; they are there only if you would like the shape of each argument in a minute rather than a full manuscript.
If you prefer a role-mapped profile snapshot, use the Short CV (and Full Glory CV for complete detail).
The one place this process led me into genuinely contentious territory is exactly that durability question. The second-best argument disarms the orthodox veto robustly for the temporary emergency brake — but extending the case to a permanent fair-rents regime is the harder, more contested step, because the emergency rationale lapses as the underlying distortions are addressed, and a durable regime therefore needs a different and more demanding foundation than the brake itself supplies. I did not set out to find that fault line; multiple independent roads led me to it. I flag it not to lecture but because locating precisely where an argument becomes contestable is the most useful thing a defender can do — and because it is the first of many nuances on which I expect your experience to correct and deepen mine.
That is the spirit in which I apply: confident in the analytical contribution, but without illusions about how much I still have to learn. That is precisely why I am applying for a relatively junior role — to learn, over time and from seasoned colleagues, the institutional, political, and practical nuances my outside-in work almost certainly underestimates. I agree with your position and want to help strengthen it from within, not argue with it.
My toolkit (MATLAB/DYNARE, STATA, Python, R, EViews) and my capacity to deliver work that holds up under scrutiny1 are ready to support NEF’s research priorities immediately. I have already identified the next empirical gaps — ground-rent-share estimation and transaction-level search-friction markups — that NEF’s proposed PRS-database expansion is positioned to close. What I bring is rigour that lowers institutional risk and a housing programme that already shows I can deliver — and a genuine hunger to learn the rest from you.
I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how I can support NEF’s mission.
Sincerely,
Carlos Galindo Escajeda

title: High Rent Isn’t Just Unaffordable. It’s Structurally Shrinking Britain’s Future.
text:
The standard account of the housing crisis is told in affordability language: rents are too high relative to incomes, and low-income households are squeezed. That framing is accurate. It is also incomplete. This paper argues that what is missing is a theory of what rent actually is — and once you have that theory, the case for a structural response becomes considerably stronger than the affordability story alone provides.
Rent, on this account, is not simply a large line item in the household budget. It is a claim on the material capacity of working households to sustain and reproduce themselves over time. That distinction matters enormously for what policy can justify.

title: High Rent Isn’t Just Unaffordable. It’s Structurally Shrinking Britain’s Future.
section: 1. What a Pound Spent on Rent Actually Takes
text:
1. What a Pound Spent on Rent Actually Takes
When a household pays rent, the money that leaves is not like money spent on anything else in the budget. It is not consumed. It does not leave behind a durable good or an enhanced capability. It transfers — from the tenant’s resources for feeding, clothing, and sustaining a family — to the landlord’s income stream.
Every pound above the minimum necessary to maintain the landlord’s participation is a pound that cannot go toward nutrition, childcare, education, health, or the basic maintenance of household capacity across generations. In political economy terms: it is a transfer from variable capital — the resources needed to reproduce the capacity to work — to ground rent. The tenant class does not simply get less disposable income. Its material capacity for social reproduction is structurally compressed.
This is not rhetorical. It follows from embedding housing costs into the logic of labor power reproduction. Population dynamics — how many workers, in what condition, are available in the next period — depend on the consumption base available for reproduction. When the rent share rises, that base shrinks. The consequence is not just a budget squeeze. It is a structural reduction in the resources available to maintain and renew the working population over time.

title: High Rent Isn’t Just Unaffordable. It’s Structurally Shrinking Britain’s Future.
section: 2. Housing Benefit Pays the Landlord, Not the Tenant
text:
2. Housing Benefit Pays the Landlord, Not the Tenant
The UK government spends over £20 billion a year on housing support. The published rationale is that this money helps low-income tenants afford homes. The empirical record is more troubling.
Gibbons and Manning (2006), using data from the 1990s UK housing benefit reforms, found that between 60% and two-thirds of the value of the benefit accrued to landlords rather than tenants — absorbed through higher rents in areas where benefit recipients were concentrated. DWP’s own econometric analysis of the 2011–12 Local Housing Allowance cuts found statistically significant rent reductions in binding areas: when the government reduced what it would pay, landlords reduced what they charged. The benefit had been functioning as a yield floor, not as an income support.
The structural reason for this is not landlord greed. It is that in areas with concentrated benefit-dependent households, the LHA rate tells landlords the maximum their tenants can pay — and the government will pay it. Landlords price to that ceiling because it is rational to do so. The subsidy does not reach the tenant as improved welfare. It reaches the landlord as income. This mechanism — fiscal capture — persists not because landlords are individually dishonest but because the market structure makes it profit-maximizing.
The companion empirical paper (Galindo 2026b) tests this directly using two natural experiments from the 2020 uplift and 2021 re-freeze of LHA rates, across 290 English local authorities and 26 analytical specifications. The reproduction-cost framework in this paper provides the structural theory of why fiscal capture is mechanically necessary — not just behaviorally observed.

title: High Rent Isn’t Just Unaffordable. It’s Structurally Shrinking Britain’s Future.
section: 3. Buy-to-Let Overvaluation Forces Rents Above the Welfare Minimum
text:
3. Buy-to-Let Overvaluation Forces Rents Above the Welfare Minimum
Post-2008 financialization pushed buy-to-let asset prices above their fundamental values. That is the empirical premise — motivated by the supply inelasticity, credit expansion, and asset-price inflation documented in the companion policy paper. Conditional on that premise, the implications for rent levels are stark.
At inflated prices, debt service on an interest-only mortgage requires a rental income above what would be necessary if the asset were priced at its fundamental value — the price consistent with a landlord earning minimum participation returns at undistorted yields. The difference between current market rents and that welfare-optimal minimum is what the paper calls the demographic externality discount.
The tenant class — excluded from buy-to-let ownership by the same capital requirements that enabled landlords to leverage into the market — cannot correct this externality through market participation. There is no mechanism by which tenants can bid the overvaluation back out of the system. The market equilibrium is structurally above the social optimum, and the gap is a necessary consequence of the asset-price inflation that the BTL expansion produced.
This is different from a standard affordability argument. It is not that landlords are charging too much by some distributional standard. It is that competitive equilibrium in this market produces rents that exceed the welfare-consistent minimum as a structural consequence of how the market was built.

title: High Rent Isn’t Just Unaffordable. It’s Structurally Shrinking Britain’s Future.
section: 4. A CPI Ceiling Is a Structural Correction, Not a Patch
text:
4. A CPI Ceiling Is a Structural Correction, Not a Patch
The reproduction framework provides the strongest possible welfare foundation for the NEF emergency brake — stronger than the generic second-best argument in the companion policy paper, which establishes that the orthodox veto is inapplicable but does not identify what rents should be.
The LPD-consistent rent is defined precisely: the minimum rent consistent with landlord participation at fundamental — non-inflated — asset prices. A CPI-anchored growth ceiling counteracts the escalating rent-to-income ratio that the overvaluation dynamic generates. It does not freeze rents at an arbitrary level. It prevents further reproduction compression by capping the pace at which rent claims on household resources can grow.
This is a structural correction aimed at the reproduction conditions of the working population. It answers the question the affordability framing cannot: not just “are rents too high?” but “what should rents be, as a matter of social welfare?” — and the answer is that the welfare-consistent ceiling is the one that allows landlord participation without the overvaluation premium that financialization has built into the market.
The framework additionally predicts that binding areas — those where LHA concentrated benefit-dependent households at high intensity — should show differential household formation and demographic patterns compared with non-binding areas. These discriminating tests remain an open empirical frontier: they are what would distinguish this structural account from a simpler behavioral story about landlords following the LHA rate.

Based on the working paper “Rent as Reproduction Cost” (2026).

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
text:
Mainstream economics has a favorite story: competitive markets solve an optimization problem, and the solution is — by the model’s own internal logic — the best of all possible worlds. Resources flow efficiently. Risk is priced correctly. If inequality persists, it is because people started with different endowments, not because the system itself compounds that difference.
We wrote a paper that takes that story’s own formal machinery — Bellman equations, Euler conditions, stochastic discount factors, second-order perturbations — and uses it to prove the story is false. Not in the hand-waving way external critics are usually dismissed for. False by the system’s own derivations, from its own premises, in its own mathematical grammar.
The result is a materialist theory of value, risk, and finance where labor-power reproduction is the fundamental numéraire. In this framework, competitive markets generate structurally necessary violations of labor’s welfare — not despite solving their optimization problem, but precisely because they solve it perfectly.
Here are seven things this paper establishes that mainstream finance theory cannot tell you.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 1. Every mainstream growth model is missing a term — and it’s not a technicality
text:
1. Every mainstream growth model is missing a term — and it’s not a technicality
The reproduction technology at the heart of our paper is simple but profound: future labor power depends on both current labor power and current consumption, with exponents that sum to one — constant returns to scale. This is the minimal formal requirement for any society that reproduces itself.
When you take this seriously, a term appears in the Euler equation that has no counterpart in any Ramsey-Cass-Koopmans model: the demographic continuation term. It governs how powerfully today’s labor force carries forward into tomorrow. The higher this term, the more today’s capital inequality compounds into future labor-power deficits.
Prior heterodox formalizations of the materialist hard core either dropped this term or introduced it inconsistently, inadvertently breaking the constant-returns structure that makes the whole framework tractable. Prior stochastic variants dropped it entirely, which quietly destroys the scale invariance of the reproduction technology and voids the derivation. The mainstream never needed to worry about it, because mainstream models don’t treat labor-power reproduction as an objective at all.
This isn’t a minor fix. Without the demographic continuation term, there is no structural risk premium with a signed demographic coefficient, no exact normalization of the value function, and no mathematical object for our welfare criterion to violate. The entire edifice stands or falls with it.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 2. We didn’t build a rival model. We turned the mainstream’s apparatus against itself.
text:
2. We didn’t build a rival model. We turned the mainstream’s apparatus against itself.
Most critiques of neoclassical economics build something different — post-Keynesian, agent-based, or classical input-output models. This paper does something rarer.
We call our strategy methodological immanence: we enter the competitive equilibrium framework on its own terms, accept its Bellman apparatus, and ask what the equilibrium can be shown to prove about itself from its own first-order conditions.
The change this requires is not technical. It is ontological. Mainstream macro asks: how do atomistic individuals optimize their subjective utility? The materialist framework asks: what does the economy require to reproduce the collective capacity to labor? These are not different ways of approaching the same question. They are different theories of what an economy is, who its subjects are, and what value means. The stochastic discount factor, the Bellman equations, and the second-order perturbation technique are all the same. But when labor-power reproduction displaces subjective utility as the fundamental primitive, the demographic continuation term reappears in the Euler equation, the pricing kernel acquires a second structural risk channel, and the welfare criterion that makes visible what competitive equilibria fail to achieve can be stated precisely.
This immanent proof establishes what external critiques cannot. The failure is not contingent on market imperfections, regulatory capture, or financial fragility. It is structurally necessary — a deduction from the competitive equilibrium’s own first-order conditions, on its own ground, against its own standard of proof.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 3. The risk premium on capital has two channels — one of them is demographic
text:
3. The risk premium on capital has two channels — one of them is demographic
Standard consumption-based asset pricing says risky assets earn a premium because they pay off poorly when consumption falls. That channel exists here too.
But our framework reveals a second channel no mainstream model contains: a demographic risk channel. An asset that performs badly precisely when society’s reproductive capacity contracts earns an additional premium. The coefficient on this channel — what we call Omega — is analytically signed positive under two mild, economically interpretable conditions about the curvature of the value function and the savings response to technology shocks.
This is not a free parameter added to fit the data. It emerges directly from the structure of the Bellman problem once the demographic continuation term is present. The pricing kernel responds to reproductive risk because the shadow value of capital that appears in the kernel is the Bellman multiplier governing reproductive capacity itself — not subjective utility. Change the primitive, and the kernel changes.
The macroeconomic implication is stark: when uncertainty about future labor power rises, precautionary demand drives up the price of safe assets and crowds out real investment. Finance does not appear here as a neutral intermediary; it is the institutional form through which the risk of future labor-power deficits is priced and redistributed across dynasties.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 4. The risk price cannot be calibrated away
text:
4. The risk price cannot be calibrated away
Mainstream asset pricing has a famous flexibility problem: its effective risk-aversion coefficient is a free parameter. It can match almost any observed equity premium simply by turning a dial.
The materialist framework has no such flexibility. The effective risk-aversion coefficient is pinned down by a cross-equation restriction that ties it to four observables:

The reproduction elasticity (identifiable from cohort fertility data)
The Bellman curvature of the value function (pinned by steady-state conditions)
The capital-ratio savings response (recoverable from investment-share dynamics)
The normalized consumption response to technology shocks

This makes the materialist framework a testable structural prediction. Standard CCAPM can match any risk premium by turning a dial; this framework cannot. If the observed risk premium is inconsistent with the reproduction technology parameters, the model is falsified — not rescued by recalibration. A theory that cannot be falsified by data is not a scientific theory; this one can be.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 5. Perfect markets still fail labor — and fail it persistently
text:
5. Perfect markets still fail labor — and fail it persistently
Our welfare criterion replaces Pareto efficiency — and the replacement is not cosmetic.
Pareto efficiency accepts preferences as given and asks whether they can be simultaneously satisfied. But preferences are themselves shaped by class position. A worker’s preference for immediate consumption over deferred investment is not a natural datum; it is a consequence of wage dependence and constrained reproduction under conditions of necessity. A welfare criterion built on such preferences takes the class structure as its own foundation and then evaluates allocations on that basis. It cannot, by design, evaluate whether the structure itself is adequate. It is an apology for a prior inequality dressed in the language of optimality.
LPD does not ask whether preferences are satisfied. It asks whether the physical preconditions for the reproduction of the labor force are met, for every dynasty, under every allocation.

Labor-Power Dominance (LPD): Allocation A dominates Allocation B if every dynasty ends up with at least as much discounted expected labor power, and at least one dynasty is strictly better off. The criterion ranks allocations directly over physical reproductive capacity — not over utility.

Under LPD, competitive markets fail systematically whenever initial capital is unequally distributed. This is not a crisis result or a market-failure result. It holds in the cleanest possible competitive benchmark: complete markets, full insurance against idiosyncratic shocks, and perfectly competitive factor pricing.
The capital-rich dynasty grows its labor force faster — not because it is more productive at reproduction, but because it consumes more, and consumption is an input to reproduction with a positive elasticity. The demographic continuation term turns this into a permanent, multiplicative growth-rate differential: each period of advantage multiplies into the next, so the ratio of labor-power levels between dynasties is strictly increasing over time.
Credit markets, labor markets, and wage equalization all fail to restore LPD. They reorganize the hierarchy; they do not dissolve it.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 6. Capitalism turns future human beings into a financial asset class
text:
6. Capitalism turns future human beings into a financial asset class
The paper closes a formal gap that Harvey, Foley, and the circuit-of-capital tradition identified but could not close without dynamic stochastic methods: the derivation of asset prices directly from the conditions of labor-power reproduction.
The safe bond is priced by the same demographic stochastic discount factor that prices risky capital. Its yield is lower precisely because it insures against reproductive-risk variance. Demand for safe assets surges when uncertainty about future labor power rises. The bond aggregates the cost of missing insurance markets across dynasties, and in doing so it prices the future reproductive capacity of society as if it were a financial claim.
This is fictitious capital in its structural form — not in the narrow Marxian sense of capitalized surplus value, but in the broader sense: an asset whose price capitalizes a ranked structure of claims on future social labor through the material conditions of reproduction. The precautionary demand that fills financial balance sheets with “safe” assets is, at its structural foundation, demand for insurance against the risk that society will not reproduce enough labor power to service those claims.
Finance, in this framework, is not an aberration, a parasite, or an external distortion imposed on an otherwise sound productive base. It is constitutive. The capitalist system generates reproductive insecurity through the unequal distribution of the means of subsistence — and then converts that insecurity into yield-bearing claims on future social labor. It produces the condition and sells insurance against it. The terror of reproductive failure is not incidental to capitalist finance; it is its raw material, converted into yield.

title: We Took Capitalism’s Own Math and Proved It Fails Labor — By Succeeding Perfectly
section: 7. This is a research program, not a closed result
text:
7. This is a research program, not a closed result
The paper is theoretical. It establishes the structural restrictions and the welfare violations. The empirical and institutional work follows in a companion research program:

Empirical identification: GMM moment conditions confronting the cross-equation restriction with cohort fertility data, normalized consumption series, and asset-pricing moments.
Class dynamics: A fully specified heterogeneous-agent model separating liquidity-constrained working dynasties from accumulating capitalist dynasties, to derive the full distributional consequences of the LPD violation.
Axiomatics: Formally mapping Labor-Power Dominance against Paretian and utilitarian criteria.

One final point for readers who know the heterodox literature. The stationarity assumption the framework requires — the ergodic structure of dynamic programming — is the price of admission for an immanent critique. It is a mathematical requirement to prove failure from within the mainstream’s own apparatus, not a historical claim that capitalism is actually stable. The stationary pricing kernel is the benchmark that any future extension incorporating crisis dynamics, class transitions, or non-ergodic reproductive trajectories must be consistent with.
Even in its most idealized, efficient, stationary form, capitalism fails labor — not by failing to optimize, but by succeeding.

title: The Economists Told You Rent Control Would Fail. They Were Measuring the Wrong Market.
text:
The lowest-income fifth of private renters in England is spending 48.5 pence in every pound of net income on housing costs. The standard economic response is: don’t cap rents, build more homes. The argument is familiar. The question this paper asks is simpler and more uncomfortable: is that argument even about the same market we have?
The answer is no.

title: The Economists Told You Rent Control Would Fail. They Were Measuring the Wrong Market.
section: 1. The Benchmark Has Conditions. Britain Fails Every One of Them.
text:
1. The Benchmark Has Conditions. Britain Fails Every One of Them.
The textbook case against rent controls is not wrong. In a genuinely competitive rental market — elastic supply, many competing landlords, prices that reflect demand rather than leverage — a binding rent ceiling can misallocate units, compress new supply, and hurt the very people it was meant to protect.
Those mechanisms are real. The problem is the small print.
The textbook conclusion depends on five conditions holding simultaneously: supply that can expand when demand rises; easy entry for competing landlords; prices that reflect genuine market conditions rather than speculation; housing used primarily as shelter rather than as a leveraged financial asset; and credit markets that are not inflating demand and detaching prices from the cost of providing homes.
Britain’s private rented sector fails every single one of them. Not marginally — structurally and by design.
Planning restrictions have blocked new supply for decades and created a persistent gap between what construction costs and what tenants pay. The Housing Act 1988 stripped tenants of security of tenure and fair-rent protection — not to create a more competitive market, but to build a sector organised around landlord pricing power and easy tenant displacement. The buy-to-let boom, which began with the first interest-only mortgage products in 1996, transformed rental property into a leveraged asset class. By 2022, approximately 85% of outstanding buy-to-let mortgages issued by major UK banks were interest-only — leaving the landlord class structurally dependent on perpetual rent escalation to service debt while sitting on assets inflated by a decade of near-zero interest rates.
This is not a neutral market that has organically evolved to its current state. It was built, in three deliberate statutory moves, to function as an investment vehicle. The competitive benchmark was never its operating logic.

title: The Economists Told You Rent Control Would Fail. They Were Measuring the Wrong Market.
section: 2. The San Francisco Study Is Being Applied to the Wrong Design
text:
2. The San Francisco Study Is Being Applied to the Wrong Design
The most frequently invoked empirical evidence against rent regulation is Diamond, McQuade, and Qian’s (2019) study of a 1994 San Francisco measure. It found reduced rental supply, tenant lock-in, and welfare losses. The finding is important. It is also routinely misapplied.
The San Francisco system was a vacancy-decontrol system: rents were controlled while a tenancy lasted, but landlords could reset rents to market levels the moment a tenancy ended. That created a direct financial incentive to remove sitting tenants. Landlords had every reason to find ways to displace households in order to recapture the accumulated gap between controlled and market rents. The result was predictable — and measured precisely.
The NEF proposal does the opposite. It prohibits vacancy decontrol entirely. Rents cannot reset when a tenancy ends. The eviction jackpot disappears at the architectural level. The specific mechanism that Diamond et al. documented and quantified is blocked by design.
Citing San Francisco as the verdict on the NEF proposal is not applying the evidence. It is ignoring the one design difference the evidence itself says was decisive.

title: The Economists Told You Rent Control Would Fail. They Were Measuring the Wrong Market.
section: 3. Rent Prices a Quadruple Object. The Standard Model Only Sees One.
text:
3. Rent Prices a Quadruple Object. The Standard Model Only Sees One.
The orthodox critique of rent regulation treats rent as the price of a current housing service — supply and demand, allocation and efficiency. That framing describes a market housing never quite was, and certainly is not now.
In the UK PRS, rent is simultaneously four things: the price of shelter; the income stream backing a capitalised asset whose value is set by the formula price-equals-rent-over-interest-rate; the cash flow servicing leveraged buy-to-let debt at interest-only terms; and the vehicle by which public housing benefit is transmitted from the state to private landlords rather than remaining with tenants.
That quadruple role is not an academic observation. It changes the policy stakes completely. When rent also anchors asset prices and leveraged expectations, capping rent growth does not merely disrupt a competitive allocation. It compresses the speculative premium that has been capitalised into property values since 2008. It interrupts a pipeline that runs from tenant income through landlord cash flows into inflated asset valuations. That pipeline was built by statute. Breaking it is not market interference — there is no competitive equilibrium here to protect.
This is the Ontological Disconnect at the heart of the rent control debate. The orthodox argument models housing as a one-object competitive service market. The UK PRS is a four-object financialised asset system. A benchmark designed for the first cannot govern the second without first proving that the four roles are separable. They are not.

title: The Economists Told You Rent Control Would Fail. They Were Measuring the Wrong Market.
section: 4. The Emergency Brake — and the Three Conditions That Must Come With It
text:
4. The Emergency Brake — and the Three Conditions That Must Come With It
The New Economics Foundation’s proposal caps annual rent increases at the lower of CPI or 2%, with no vacancy decontrol and an exemption for newly built homes. Each element has a structural purpose. The growth ceiling — rather than a level freeze — preserves current landlord cash flows while ending rent escalation, avoiding the immediate exit pressure that Scotland’s harder freeze design produced. The no-vacancy-decontrol clause closes the eviction jackpot. The new-build exemption protects the supply margin that actually creates new housing.
But a rent brake alone is not enough. The housing crisis has three structural drivers, and it requires three simultaneous responses.
Supply must expand. Planning restrictions are not incidental — they are one of the main mechanisms by which scarcity value has been systematically transferred from renters to landowners. England needs to build at scale. The current target of 300,000 net completions per year has never been met; meeting it is a precondition for the brake to be genuinely temporary rather than permanent.
Land-value gains must be captured. Supply expansion without land-value capture can enrich developers and landowners before it helps tenants. Every major upzoning decision creates a windfall. Public capture mechanisms — whether through planning obligations, community land trusts, or local authority acquisition — are what ensure those gains return to the public rather than being absorbed into the same asset-inflation cycle the brake is trying to interrupt.
The brake must have statutory exit criteria. A rent cap whose justification rests on temporary market failure must not harden into a permanent settlement. The paper proposes measurable thresholds: the housing-cost burden of the bottom income quintile falls below 30% for two consecutive annual releases of official statistics; net housing completions in England exceed 300,000 per year; and a functioning successor fair-rents system with real monitoring and quality standards is in place. Pre-committed exit rules do two jobs: they make the brake credible as an emergency instrument rather than a political convenience, and they protect tenants from the revolving discretion that destabilised Scotland’s experiment.
Britain’s renters are already in the emergency. The question is whether the response matches the market as it actually exists.

title: Before the Housing Work: Microsimulating Anti-Poverty Policy in Mexico
text: Earlier, pre-AI research — and separate from the five-paper UK housing programme on this site. These two peer-reviewed papers (in Spanish, 2010, with Celina Escajeda and Oscar Galindo) are the early-career work the application refers to: the first time I taught myself survey microdata and the microsimulation literature from a standing start, and carried it through to publication.

title: Before the Housing Work: Microsimulating Anti-Poverty Policy in Mexico
text:
The question
In 2010, with two colleagues at the Universidad Autónoma Chapingo, I took up a question that turns out to be the same one NEF asks about Britain: how is poverty actually distributed across a population, and what would a given policy do to it? The setting was the State of Mexico — the country’s most populous — and the raw material was the national household income and expenditure survey, ENIGH 2008: a large, stratified, clustered sample, with roughly 2,480 of its households falling in the state we cared about.
The work split into two papers, and they answer two different questions. The first asks how you should measure poverty before you say anything about it — what you count, where you draw the line, and how sure you are. The second asks the harder, policy-facing question: if you could change one thing about a household, how much poverty would move, and for whom? Each gets its own explainer below.

title: Before the Housing Work: Microsimulating Anti-Poverty Policy in Mexico
section: Explainer 1 · Measuring poverty before explaining it
text:
Explainer 1 · Measuring poverty before explaining it
Before you can argue about whether a place is poor, you have to settle three things that most poverty statistics leave unspoken: what you measure, where you draw the line, and how sure you are of the answer. Almost all of the disagreement in the field hides inside those three choices. This first paper is about getting them right before drawing any conclusion at all — because a finding is only as honest as the choices that produced it.

Measure what people spend, not what they say they earn
We built the welfare measure from consumption — what each household actually spends per person in a month, deflated to a common August-2008 price base — rather than from reported income. That is a deliberate departure from the income-based headlines most poverty debates run on.
The reasoning is practical and slightly counter-intuitive. Incomes are lumpy, seasonal, and under-reported, especially at the bottom of the distribution, where an informal wage or a bad month never shows up cleanly on a survey form. Spending is steadier: households smooth it across good months and bad, and it tracks the standard of living a family can actually sustain rather than the one a single pay-cycle happens to imply.
Choosing the ruler is not a technicality — it decides who counts as poor before any policy argument begins. A consumption measure pulls the count toward households whose realised welfare is low, not merely those whose reported income dipped in the survey week. That is precisely the population an anti-poverty policy is trying to reach, and getting it wrong at this step quietly biases everything downstream.


Don’t trust one poverty line — test every line at once
The usual fight in poverty measurement is over the line. Set it a little higher or lower and the headline number moves, so the argument quietly becomes about the threshold instead of about the place. Mexico’s official CONEVAL lines are one defensible choice among many, and committing to any single number invites the obvious objection that you picked the cut-off that gave you the answer you wanted.
So we refused the choice. Instead of selecting one line and defending it, we compared the State of Mexico against the rest of the country across the whole continuum of plausible lines, using first-order stochastic dominance. The question stops being “is it poorer at this line?” and becomes “is it poorer at every line at once?” A household is no longer simply poor or not poor by one official verdict; the comparison holds across the entire range a reasonable person might choose.
That is a stronger claim than any single statistic, and a more honest one. When one distribution dominates another at every threshold, the conclusion no longer depends on where anyone draws the line — which takes the very thing critics usually attack, the cut-off, off the table entirely.


Put honest error bars on a survey that isn’t simple
ENIGH is not a simple random sample. It is stratified, clustered, and weighted — built to be efficient and representative, not to make a statistician’s life easy. A standard error computed as though the data were a clean random draw would understate the true uncertainty, sometimes badly, and a poverty gap that looks decisive on paper can dissolve once the design is taken seriously.
So we carried the survey’s design through the statistics, using Huber linearisation, and reported the result not as a single test but as confidence bands running along the entire range of lines. For any threshold, you can see at a glance whether the gap between the state and the rest of the country is real or within noise. The uncertainty is quantified across the whole comparison, not asserted once at a convenient point — which is the difference between a result you can stand behind and one you merely hope holds.


The finding
Across that range, the State of Mexico carried a statistically significant excess of urban poverty — between 7 and 13 percentage points above the rest of the country. In people, that is on the order of 0.9 to 1.9 million more poor than the national pattern alone would predict.
The width of that band is the honesty: it is what the data genuinely support once you stop pretending the line and the sampling are free choices. But even at its lower edge, the gap is too large, and too stable across every threshold, to be an artefact of where anyone chose to draw the line. The country’s most populous state was carrying a concentration of urban poverty that the national average quietly absorbed and hid — exactly the kind of thing careful measurement is for.

title: Before the Housing Work: Microsimulating Anti-Poverty Policy in Mexico
section: Explainer 2 · Simulating a policy, household by household
text:
Explainer 2 · Simulating a policy, household by household
Measurement tells you where poverty is. It does not tell you what would move it. The second paper takes the step that matters for policy: building a model you can run experiments on, then asking it what each lever is actually worth — and, crucially, who it reaches.

Turn “are you poor?” into a probability
The move that makes everything else possible is to stop treating poverty as a yes-or-no verdict at a single line. We estimated a model of household consumption from each household’s characteristics — the schooling and employment of the head, transfers, remittances, location, and the rest — fitted to the survey with its design weights, so the better-off and the harder-to-reach both count for the right amount.
Once you have that model, you can read off, for any household and any line, the probability that it falls below it. A household is no longer simply poor or not poor; it carries a 20% chance, or an 80% chance, of being under a given line — and a policy is whatever shifts that probability.
The poverty rate of a whole group then becomes the average of those probabilities. That small reframing is what turns a static photograph of poverty into something you can intervene on and re-measure: a model, not just a number.


Change one thing, and recompute everyone
With the model in hand, you can simulate. Take every household head with no schooling, give them some, hold everything else fixed, recompute the probabilities, and read off how far poverty falls — for the population as a whole and for each subgroup separately.
That yields what the paper calls the implicit return of a policy action: the share of existing poverty a given intervention would erase if you could deliver it. It is the same logic the macro-micro literature of Ravallion and Bourguignon uses — push a defined change through household microdata and read the distributional consequence directly, rather than collapsing it into one national average that tells you nothing about who was helped.
It is a clean accounting, not a forecast. You are not predicting the future of the economy; you are asking the survey itself, household by household, what a specific lever is worth — and getting an answer with a distribution attached.


Be honest about what it can’t say
This is deliberately a first-round, non-behavioural calculation. It holds other behaviour fixed: it does not model the labour market re-adjusting, prices moving, or families changing what they do once the policy lands. So it answers a precise question — “who gains immediately, and by how much” — and it is explicit that the answer only holds for changes small enough not to disturb everything else.
Naming that boundary is part of the method, not an apology for it. A first-round estimate that is honest about being first-round is more useful than a grand general-equilibrium story whose extra moving parts you can neither see nor check. The discipline — and it is the same discipline the UK housing papers run on — is claiming exactly what the data support, and not one inch more.


What actually moves the needle
The strongest lever by far was the education of the household head. Simulating a move from no schooling to some cut the probability of being poor by more than 30% in some subgroups — a larger effect than any other single change we tested, and robust enough to survive the honest error bars rather than washing out inside them.
The rest were real but smaller. The head’s employment, government transfers, remittances, the head’s health, and indigenous status each moved poverty by somewhere between roughly 0.5% and 23%, depending heavily on which group you looked at. The heterogeneity was the point, not a nuisance: a lever that barely registers on the national average can be decisive for one subpopulation and almost irrelevant for another. That is precisely the information a policymaker needs in order to target, and precisely the information a single headline number destroys.
Read those two papers together and the shape of the later work is already there — measure carefully before explaining, test a finding across every threshold, then change one thing and report who it reaches rather than whether it “works” on average.

title: Before the Housing Work: Microsimulating Anti-Poverty Policy in Mexico
section: Why both papers are on this site
text:
Why both papers are on this site
Two reasons. First, this is the earliest version of the craft the housing application rests on: teaching myself relational survey microdata, complex sampling, and a simulation literature from scratch, and carrying all of it through to peer review. The instinct on display — measure before you explain, refuse the convenient threshold, change one thing and read off who it helps — is the same instinct behind the UK housing programme, fifteen years on.
Second, it predates today’s AI tooling entirely. The method, the judgement, and the mistakes were done by hand, years before any of these tools existed. It is not part of the five-paper UK housing programme; it is where the habits behind that programme were formed.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
text:
The UK government spends over £20 billion a year on housing support. The official claim: this money helps low-income people afford their homes. The empirical reality, now measured with government data across 290 English local authorities and two policy experiments, tells a different story. Much of it ends up with landlords.
Not through fraud. Not through individual bad actors. Through a structural mechanism that has been embedded in the design of Local Housing Allowance since its introduction — and that two natural experiments, across 26 different analytical methods, now confirm.
Here is what we found, and what it means.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
section: 1. The Floor That Moves the Ceiling
text:
1. The Floor That Moves the Ceiling
In areas where many tenants rely on housing benefit, the Local Housing Allowance (LHA) does not operate as a helping hand. It operates as a price anchor. Landlords set rents at or near the LHA rate because they know two things: that is the maximum their tenants can pay, and the government will pay it.
The consequence is fiscal capture: the public transfer that is nominally for tenants structurally accrues to property owners. When the LHA goes up, rents follow. When it is frozen, rent growth slows. The benefit does not improve the tenant’s position — it improves the landlord’s revenue.
This is not a new claim. Gibbons and Manning (2006) found that 60–67% of UK housing benefit accrues to landlords rather than tenants, using data from the 1990s reforms. DWP’s own econometric analysis of the 2011–12 LHA cuts confirmed rent reductions in the areas most affected. What has been missing is direct, high-resolution evidence from the most recent policy cycle — and a theory that explains why the mechanism persists even in a nominally competitive rental market.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
text:
2. Parliament Accidentally Ran Two Experiments
Governments rarely provide economists with clean natural experiments. The 2020–21 LHA policy cycle is a rare exception.
April 2020: After years of freezing LHA below market rents, the government restored it to the 30th percentile of local market rents — the largest uprating since 2016. If fiscal capture is real, rents in high-benefit areas should have accelerated immediately. Landlords could charge more because their tenants’ budgets had just expanded.
April 2021: LHA was re-frozen at the 2020 cash level, while market rents continued rising. If fiscal capture is real, rent growth in those same areas should have decelerated — the floor was now being held below the rising market, and the yield advantage of binding areas should fade.
Both predictions come true in the data. Areas with higher concentrations of LHA-dependent households saw rent growth accelerate at the 2020 uplift and decelerate at the 2021 re-freeze — exactly as the fiscal capture theory predicts, and exactly opposite to what you would observe if LHA were operating as a neutral income support rather than a price anchor.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
section: 3. We Checked 26 Different Ways. The Answer Was Always the Same.
text:
3. We Checked 26 Different Ways. The Answer Was Always the Same.
A single finding can always be dismissed: statistical noise, a convenient choice of time window, a sample that was selected to produce the desired result. We therefore ran 26 different versions of the analysis — varying:

The time window (different start and end dates, including a version that uses the 2020 uplift period itself as the comparison baseline)
Whether to control for post-COVID urban density recovery
Whether to restrict the sample to lower-migration areas
The bedroom type (1-bed, 2-bed, 3-bed, 4-bed separately)
Whether to down-weight large local authorities
Whether to treat the treatment variable as continuous or as a binary threshold
The clustering of standard errors

Across all 26 analyses — temporal, spatial, compositional, measurement — every single estimated effect points in the same direction. Zero sign reversals. This is not cherry-picking; it is structural consistency. The fiscal capture pattern persists under every analytical lens.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
text:
4. It Is Not Displacement
The most common objection to this kind of finding is that the pattern reflects population displacement, not fiscal capture. As LHA is frozen and real incomes fall, lower-income households move out of high-benefit areas. Rents “slow” because the remaining tenants are wealthier — not because landlords are responding to the LHA rate.
We tested this directly. We excluded the 30 English local authorities with the highest rates of net in-migration — the places most likely to be experiencing significant population churn — and re-ran the analysis on the remaining 261 areas. The result did not disappear. It got slightly stronger: the estimated effect is more negative in non-displacement areas than in the full sample.
Fiscal capture is not a displacement artefact. It operates in areas where the population is stable. It is structural, not compositional.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
section: 5. The Headline Number Is a Lower Bound
text:
5. The Headline Number Is a Lower Bound
The primary estimate — roughly a 1.7 percentage point reduction in rent growth per unit of LHA intensity — may sound modest. Two features of the study design guarantee it is an underestimate.
First, landlords are reluctant to cut nominal rents even when their LHA floor retreats below the market. This downward nominal rigidity attenuates the measured effect of the re-freeze, particularly in the early quarters after April 2021.
Second, in dense urban areas — which are also high-LHA-intensity areas — post-COVID demand for private renting surged for reasons entirely unrelated to LHA policy. This independent demand recovery in binding areas partially masks the rent deceleration from the freeze.
When we strip out both sources of attenuation — by using the 2020 uplift period as the comparison baseline (which identifies the predicted reversal from accelerated growth at the uplift to decelerated growth at the re-freeze) and controlling explicitly for urban density recovery — the estimated effect is roughly four times larger. That is the fiscal capture signal, isolated from the noise.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
text:
6. The Reproduction Trap
The Labor-Power as Numéraire (LPN) framework provides the theoretical grounding for why this mechanism is not merely a market distortion but a structural feature of the UK housing economy.
Housing costs for benefit-dependent households are not just a consumption expenditure — they are inputs to social reproduction. The capacity to work, to form households, to raise children requires that non-housing consumption — food, childcare, transport, heating — remain above a threshold. LHA in high-benefit areas is not primarily a housing supplement; it is a reproduction subsidy maintaining that threshold.
When LHA is frozen and market rents continue rising, the real value of that subsidy falls. The rent deceleration we measure is not merely landlords receiving slightly less revenue — it is the reproduction constraint tightening on the least economically secure households in England. Households do not simply substitute away from housing; they face compressing capacity across all non-housing necessities simultaneously.
The LPN framework predicts that the fiscal capture mechanism should therefore produce demographic consequences — slower household formation, slower population growth — in high-intensity areas after the re-freeze, independently of the rent growth deceleration itself. Testing that prediction is the next step in this research programme.

title: Your Housing Benefit Is Going to Your Landlord. We Can Now Measure How Much.
text:
What Comes Next
The finding is clear: LHA cannot be reformed in isolation. As long as housing benefit can be freely capitalised into rents, raising the benefit raises rents, and the net benefit to tenants approaches zero. The Gibbons–Manning finding from 2006 — that the majority of housing benefit flows to landlords — has now been confirmed with updated, high-resolution data across the most recent policy cycle.
Two changes are necessary together. First, a rent ceiling calibrated to the LHA rate in binding local authorities — not a blanket national freeze, but a binding constraint on LHA-anchored tenancies that prevents landlords from extracting above the benefit in areas where fiscal capture is confirmed. Second, reformed LHA design that supplements tenant consumption directly rather than subsidising landlord revenue flows through the rent mechanism.
Neither change is straightforward. Both are politically contested. But the evidence that they are necessary — 290 local authorities, two natural experiments, 26 empirical tests, consistent direction — is now on the table.
The housing benefit was designed to help people who cannot afford market rents. The data now says it has been, in large part, helping their landlords instead. That is a political choice. It can be made differently.

title: We Built a Research Programme. Then We Tried to Break It. Here’s What Survived.
text:
Heterodox economics rarely gets a fair hearing. Its premises are dismissed at the threshold — too political, too unconventional, insufficiently neutral — without anyone pausing to ask whether the body of work has actually been developing in a disciplined and progressive way. The question of whether a heterodox programme is internally rigorous — whether it is generating new content rather than papering over anomalies — is simply never reached.
This paper insists on reaching that question for a specific four-paper sequence on labour power, housing, and value. Not to endorse it. Not to prove it true. To audit it fairly.

title: We Built a Research Programme. Then We Tried to Break It. Here’s What Survived.
text:
1. Four Papers, One Argument
The sequence at stake consists of four pieces that work together as one argument distributed across four different analytical levels.
A theory paper takes the reproduction of labour power — rather than subjective consumer preferences — as the primitive from which value is reckoned, and replaces the standard welfare criterion of Pareto efficiency with one it calls Labor-Power Dominance. A structural paper derives from that criterion a welfare-consistent ceiling on rent, and identifies the mechanisms by which buy-to-let financialization forces rents above that ceiling. An empirical paper tests, across 290 English local authorities and two natural experiments, whether housing benefit is being captured by landlords rather than reaching tenants. A policy paper argues that the standard economic objection to rent regulation is inapplicable to the market Britain actually has.
These are not four separate arguments about related topics. They share a single hard core — the claim that labour power reproduction is the fundamental unit of social value — and address four different implications of that core. Strip out the connecting tissue and each paper becomes weaker. Read together, they constitute a coherent programme.

title: We Built a Research Programme. Then We Tried to Break It. Here’s What Survived.
section: 2. The Lakatosian Test — and Why It’s the Right One
text:
2. The Lakatosian Test — and Why It’s the Right One
The philosopher of science Imre Lakatos distinguished between two kinds of research programme development. A degenerating programme, when it faces a challenge, adds an untestable auxiliary hypothesis to patch the anomaly — rescuing the core at the cost of making the programme less falsifiable. A progressing programme, by contrast, responds to challenges by revising its protective belt in ways that reduce the programme’s degrees of freedom and increase its explanatory reach. Genuine progress is measured by whether the belt revision restricts the modeller rather than giving them more room.
The paper applies this framework to the four-paper sequence and delivers a deliberately split verdict.
The programme is theoretically progressive. The most important revision in the sequence converted an unproven conjecture about demographic risk — introduced to address a specific anomaly in the formal model — into a signed, closed-form restriction tied to four independently observable parameters. That revision did not add flexibility. It subtracted it. The coefficient that had been a free conjecture became derivable from conditions with empirical content. That is the structural opposite of an ad hoc rescue.
The programme is non-degenerating. Under recorded attacks on the hard core itself — challenges to the most fundamental commitments — the core was preserved through principled refusal and belt revision, not by inventing new untestable claims. The standard of proof required is that the core stays fixed while the belt absorbs and responds to pressure. That standard was met.
But the programme is empirically progressing, not yet empirically progressive. This is the honest part.

title: We Built a Research Programme. Then We Tried to Break It. Here’s What Survived.
section: 3. The Result That Couldn’t Be Claimed — and Why That Matters
text:
3. The Result That Couldn’t Be Claimed — and Why That Matters
The highest standard of Lakatosian progress requires not merely corroboration but corroboration of a novel prediction — a result that the programme predicts and its rivals do not, and that the rivals’ alternative account cannot accommodate after the fact.
The fiscal capture finding — that housing benefit is captured by landlords rather than reaching tenants — looks at first glance like exactly this kind of result. The reproduction framework predicts it structurally, not just behaviorally. The empirical paper confirms it across 26 different analytical specifications with zero sign reversals. That is an unusually robust finding.
The paper’s own methodological discipline required that this result be demoted. The problem is observational equivalence: a simpler behavioral story — landlords follow the LHA rate — predicts the same empirical pattern. The reproduction framework’s prediction is not, in this instance, a genuinely novel prediction that discriminates the programme from its rival. It is shared content. Both the programme and a much simpler story predict fiscal capture.
The paper demotes its own strongest-looking result rather than claim credit for it. This is unusual in academic economics, where the incentive runs powerfully in the other direction.
What remains as the genuine discriminating frontier are the programme’s demographic predictions: that binding areas, with higher concentrations of LHA-dependent households, should show differential household formation rates and population dynamics compared with non-binding areas. Those tests are registered, explicitly falsifiable, and still open.

title: We Built a Research Programme. Then We Tried to Break It. Here’s What Survived.
section: 4. What This Means for the Hiring Package
text:
4. What This Means for the Hiring Package
For a research role at NEF, the methodological point of this paper is also a practical one. The programme demonstrates its credibility not only by accumulating positive results but by its willingness to demote convenient findings when they do not meet the standard it claims to hold. That discipline is the foundation on which policy recommendations can be trusted.
A programme that claims to have proven more than it has is politically useful in the short term and fragile under scrutiny. A programme that is explicit about what it has established, what remains open, and what would refute it is the kind of thing that can sustain serious advocacy. The distinction is exactly what the paper makes.
The registered discriminating tests also create a forward research agenda. If the demographic predictions are confirmed at scale — differential household formation and population growth in high-intensity binding areas — that would be genuine novel corroboration in the Lakatosian sense. It is an empirically tractable question with data that exist. It is waiting to be answered.

title: The Work Behind the Screen
text:
Carlos Galindo Escajeda · June 2026
The video on this page shows a machine producing text. That is the least interesting part of the process.
Producing text costs nothing now. Anyone can generate a draft in seconds. But a draft is not research. Left to itself, a machine pulls a sharp argument back toward the conventional. The real work is not generating the output. It is governing the machine that produces it.
In a quixotesque way, the machine is tireless and genuinely useful — it will fetch a figure, carry an argument across three counties, and never complain. But it stays a squire. It requires a Quixote to envision and to use his imagination to lead the quest. Sancho keeps no quest of its own, and it cannot tell a giant from a windmill. Quixote supplies the vision and holds the reins; the squire does the legwork. What follows is what it takes to keep the Quixote and Sancho honest.
What you are looking at is the surface of a whole body of work. Beneath it sit five linked papers. One builds a theory of why housing costs decide whether working families can hold together across generations. Another tests that theory against real UK government data — rent indices, benefit caseloads, housing stock. A third works out what rent would have to be to leave families that room. A fourth defends a rent cap using the same mathematics mainstream economists use to oppose one. The fifth audits the whole programme and says plainly where the evidence stops.
Every figure ties to a public source you can check. Every draft was attacked on purpose — from the evidence, the logic, the framing, and the strongest case the other side could make — to find where it broke. Each draft was cross-examined by competing models, so no model marked its own homework. The machine was not careful on its own. The person running it was.
Work like this means moving between very different kinds of thinking. One problem is working out why two government datasets give clashing numbers for the same local authority; another is checking by hand whether a line of stochastic calculus actually follows from the Bellman equation above it. In between is everything else — cleaning bad data, holding an argument to a proof, and knowing which results are real and which only look it.
That range does not come from software. It comes from a career measured in decades: building models from scratch, teaching people to use data so messy it had been abandoned, and, above all, being wrong often enough that failure starts to look familiar. That experience is what lets a person read a result the way a doctor reads a scan. It catches the machine claiming more than it has shown.
The work leaves a trail.
When two official sources conflicted, the numbers were reconciled, not quietly averaged away. When a central theorem could only prove a narrow case, it was scoped back to a first-order perturbation rather than dressed up as a general law. And when the machine tried to soften a sharp idea — “KKT distortion mechanisms” — into something blander, the change was caught and reversed. Three different errors, caught by the same judgment.
That judgment also decides what to give up. When a test on migration data came back weak, it was not made to look decisive. It went into a footnote, and stronger evidence took its place: the same finding — that landlords capture much of the housing subsidy — holding across more than twenty different specifications, with no reversals.
AI tools are everywhere now. What stays rare is the judgment to know what is real, and the discipline to prove it to a reader who assumes it is not.
The knight charged windmills, certain they were giants. Here it is the other way round: the giant is real — the UK housing market — and the world has agreed to call it a windmill. Seeing that takes imagination. Proving it takes everything above. The squire never asks whether the giant is real; it charges on command and calls the day done. The asking is mine — and so is being wrong.

The point is not that a machine can produce text; it is that the system behind it had to be designed, stress-tested, and brought to the point where its output holds up — and that engineering was the author’s, built over years before any of it ran. title: Fiscal Capture in the UK PRS
text:
Abstract
This is the empirical pillar of the case NEF makes: evidence that the state’s reliance on Local Housing Allowance (LHA) partly subsidises landlords rather than protecting tenants. Using a difference-in-differences design across 290 English local authorities (2019–2024) — built from ONS private-rent indices, DWP Stat-Xplore caseloads, MHCLG dwelling-stock estimates and NOMIS wage and claimant data — it exploits two natural experiments: the April 2020 LHA uplift to the 30th percentile and the April 2021 re-freeze. If LHA acts as a binding yield floor, rent growth in high-LHA-intensity areas should accelerate at the uplift and decelerate at the re-freeze. Across 24 specifications the directional signature is consistent with capture in every case, with zero sign reversals. The paper is candid about magnitude: downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in attenuate the re-freeze response, so the headline estimate is reported deliberately as a conservative lower bound, with larger effects in the windows that isolate the mechanism more cleanly. For NEF’s advocacy the implication is concrete: because a real share of any LHA increase is absorbed into rents, raising or unfreezing LHA without a rent ceiling partly funds landlord yields — so a ceiling is a necessary complement to benefit reform, not an alternative to it. The distinguishing demographic test (whether captured areas also show slower household formation) is identified as the next empirical step, not claimed here.
