title: Fiscal Capture in the UK PRS
text:
1. Introduction
The UK Local Housing Allowance transfers public funds to low-income households to help cover private rents. Whether that transfer reaches tenants or is instead captured by landlords through rent inflation — the benefit-incidence question — is the central empirical question of this paper, and its answer has direct implications for how LHA expenditure should be evaluated as fiscal policy. Prior work establishes that landlord capture is substantial. Gibbons and Manning (2006) find that 60–67% of UK housing benefit accrues to landlords rather than tenants; Brewer et al. (2014) confirm rent reductions in binding local authorities following the 2011–12 LHA reforms. The international incidence literature establishes the same pattern: Susin (2002) finds US rent vouchers raise rents for all low-income households; Fack (2006) estimates that 78 cents of every euro of French housing benefit is absorbed in higher rents; Collinson and Ganong (2018) show that uniform voucher generosity transmits to landlords rather than tenants. Yet the standard account — landlords know their tenants’ maximum benefit and price accordingly — does not explain why this behaviour persists in the face of competition. The persistence of LHA-anchored pricing requires a structural mechanism linking LHA rates to the reproduction costs of the benefit-dependent tenant class.
The UK LHA policy of 2016–24 generates two exogenous policy events that allow direct identification of fiscal capture. In April 2016, LHA was frozen at 2015–16 cash levels, progressively unbinding the floor as market rents rose. In April 2020, the government temporarily restored LHA to the 30th percentile of local market rents. In April 2021, LHA was re-frozen at these uplifted levels while market rents continued to rise. These events create directionally opposite, testable predictions: if LHA operates as a binding yield floor, areas with higher LHA intensity should see rent growth accelerate at the uplift (the floor rises) and decelerate at the re-freeze (the floor is held below rising market rents). The two tests are not symmetrically powered. The uplift test (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{up}} > 0\)) is the higher-powered identifier because rents adjust readily to upward floor changes. The re-freeze test (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\)) is subject to two attenuation mechanisms — downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in — so a near-zero estimate is consistent with genuine fiscal capture; a significantly negative estimate constitutes strong evidence.
We quantify the LHA incidence across 290 England local authorities, exploiting both events in a difference-in-differences design. The treatment variable — LHA intensity, measured as housing benefit and Universal Credit private rented sector caseload as a share of private rental stock in 2018–19 — is pre-period and predetermined with respect to both policy events. The design uses region-by-quarter fixed effects to absorb common shocks, entity fixed effects to absorb time-invariant LA characteristics, and the NOMIS claimant count and ASHE 10th-percentile wage as time-varying controls. The 10th-percentile wage is structurally required under the LPN framework as the outside option of the benefit-dependent tenant class; we use the 10th percentile rather than the median wage for this reason.
The primary inferential claim is robust directional consistency: across 24 fiscal capture specifications varying the estimation window, spatial controls, bedroom composition, and outlier treatment, every point estimate for \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) is negative with zero sign reversals. No single methodological choice — window, density control, bedroom specification, or outlier treatment — reverses the sign. This pattern, spanning four methodologically distinct classes of specification choice, constitutes structural triangulation rather than frequentist multiplicity. The COVID-window restriction (2020-Q2–2024-Q1), which identifies the predicted fiscal-capture reversal by using the uplift period as the comparison baseline, yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0498\) (\(p = 0.0033\)); after additionally stripping post-COVID urban demand recovery via a density control, the mechanistic isolator yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0675\) (\(p = 0.0001\)). The baseline primary specification yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0174\) (\(p = 0.142\)), attenuated by construction (§2.2); it provides a lower bound. The R4 placebo (\(p = 0.562\), 2015–2019) supports parallel trends. A conservative sample restriction excluding high net in-migration local authorities yields \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0195\) (\(p = 0.119\), 261 LAs), confirming the mechanism is not purely compositional.
Two features of the design are worth noting upfront. First, the primary specification is underpowered by construction: downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in attenuate \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) precisely when fiscal capture is real, so the primary spec provides a lower bound on the effect. The COVID-window restriction and density-controlled estimates are better-powered. Second, the 24 specifications share the same 290-LA cross-section and are therefore not statistically independent. We interpret the zero-sign-reversal pattern as specification robustness — evidence that the negative sign is not an artefact of any particular window, control set, or functional form — rather than as 24 independent frequentist tests.
Beyond the fiscal capture evidence, the paper contributes a structural interpretation grounded in the Labor-Power as Numéraire (LPN) framework of Huato and Galindo (2026c). Under LPN, LHA functions as a reproduction subsidy maintaining the non-housing consumption base of benefit-dependent households along the labor-power balanced growth path. Its freeze is therefore not merely a policy choice; it is a structural compression of the demographic reproduction capacity of high-intensity local authorities. This interpretation generates an additional, distinguishable prediction: binding LAs should show not only decelerated rent growth but also slower household formation and population growth relative to non-binding areas. Testing those demographic predictions is outside the scope of this paper and is the subject of ongoing work (Galindo 2026a).
The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the institutional background. Section 3 describes the data. Section 4 presents the empirical design. Section 5 reports the main results. Section 6 presents robustness specifications. Section 7 develops the LPN structural interpretation. Section 8 discusses limitations. Section 9 concludes.

The mechanism through which LHA anchors rents operates at the level of the 152 Broad Rental Market Areas (BRMAs) into which England is divided. Within each BRMA, LHA is set at (or, during freeze periods, below) the 30th percentile of local market rents for each bedroom category, with the intention of giving benefit-dependent households access to at least the lower third of local rental supply. When LHA reaches the 30th percentile it anchors the lower bound of the active letting market: landlords with properties at or near the BRMA-level LHA rate face a soft yield floor when renting to housing benefit or Universal Credit claimants, because tenants’ housing cost allowances cap at that level. Properties priced above the LHA rate are effectively inaccessible to benefit-dependent households; properties at or below it constitute the relevant sub-market for this tenant class. The LHA rate therefore functions as a local price signal — not a legal ceiling, but a hard constraint on the budgets of a substantial share of private renters in binding BRMAs.
Figure 1 makes the receding floor concrete. Because the allowance is reset to the 30th percentile only at each uplift and then held in cash terms, it falls progressively below that percentile as market rents rise between uplifts. Through the 2021–24 re-freeze the 30th percentile of two-bedroom market rents grew at roughly seven per cent per year while the allowance grew not at all, opening a gap of approximately £106 per month: by 2024 the allowance had receded well below the bottom third of the active letting market that it is statutorily intended to cover.1 This is a descriptive comparison of the policy rule with observed market rents and carries no causal content; it identifies the policy-induced wedge whose incidence the remainder of the paper estimates.






Figure 1: The receding yield floor. Two-bedroom market rents (ONS PIPR — median and 30th percentile across England local authorities) against the Local Housing Allowance, 2015–2026. Top: levels (£/month); the allowance is reset to the 30th percentile at the April 2020 and April 2024 uplifts and frozen between, so it drifts below the rising 30th percentile during each freeze. Bottom: year-on-year growth — through each freeze the 30th percentile (the allowance’s statutory target) grows while the allowance grows zero, the divergence that accumulates into the level gap above. Shaded bands mark the 2016–20 freeze, the 2020 uplift, and the 2021–24 re-freeze; the dotted line marks the April 2024 re-linking.



The same compression bears unevenly across household sizes. Because the allowance is reset and then frozen in cash terms, the shortfall accumulated over a freeze scales with the rent level: Figure 2 shows that by 2024 the frozen allowance had fallen £88 per month below the 30th percentile for a one-bedroom home but £217 for a four-bedroom home — 2.5 times larger for family-sized accommodation, though the proportional erosion (about 15 per cent) was similar across sizes.






Figure 2: Cash shortfall by household size. For each bedroom category, the 30th-percentile market rent (ONS PIPR) at the level where the allowance was set at the April 2020 uplift (then frozen) and the level the market reached by 2024-Q1. The cash gap by which the frozen allowance fell behind the bottom third of the market rises from £88 per month for a one-bedroom home to £217 for a four-bedroom home, while the proportional erosion (about 15 per cent) is similar across sizes.



Benefit-dependent households are concentrated at the lower end of the private rental stock. In our sample, LHA intensity — housing benefit and Universal Credit private rented sector caseload as a share of the private rental stock — averages 4.4% across 294 local authorities, but is distributed unevenly: the top decile reaches intensities above 8%, concentrated in coastal towns, post-industrial northern districts, and selected inner-London boroughs outside the highest-rent BRMAs. In high-intensity local authorities, the LHA anchor price represents a larger fraction of the active letting market and landlords face stronger incentives to price at or near the maximum allowance. The expected fiscal capture signal — differential rent growth between high-intensity and low-intensity local authorities, correlated with the LHA policy cycle — is therefore most visible at the upper end of the lha_intensity distribution, and it is precisely this contrast that the difference-in-differences design exploits.
Prior evidence on LHA incidence establishes the underlying phenomenon but is limited in one specific respect. Gibbons and Manning (2006), examining the 1990s restructuring of UK housing benefit, and Brewer et al. (2014), examining the 2011–12 LHA reforms that introduced per-room rates, extended the Shared Accommodation Rate to the under-35s, and capped allowances at the 30th percentile for the first time, both identify substantial landlord capture. Both studies test only the downward rent response to a cut or freeze; neither has access to a subsequent uplift event. This paper addresses that gap by using the April 2020 uplift as a quasi-experimental baseline for the April 2021 re-freeze, permitting identification of the directional reversal — accelerated rent growth at the uplift followed by decelerated rent growth at the re-freeze in high-intensity local authorities — that is the definitive test of the yield-floor mechanism.


2.2 Why the Re-freeze Coefficient is Attenuated
The re-freeze test (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\)) is subject to two attenuation mechanisms absent from the uplift test. First, downward nominal rigidity: landlords resist cutting rents below existing levels even when the LHA yield floor recedes. Second, tenant lock-in: sitting tenants in high-LHA-intensity areas face moving costs that suppress re-negotiation during periods of general rent inflation. A near-zero \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) is therefore consistent with genuine fiscal capture; a significantly negative estimate constitutes strong evidence.
These attenuation mechanisms have a direct implication for the specification hierarchy in this paper. The primary specification (R1), which uses the full 2019-Q1 to 2024-Q1 window with the entire pre-2021-Q3 period as the comparison baseline, is most severely affected: the comparison window includes the 2019–2020 pre-uplift period, during which rent dynamics in high-intensity areas were already shaped by the ongoing 2016 freeze, compressing the measured contrast. The COVID-window restriction (R3) mitigates this by opening the window at 2020-Q2 — the start of the uplift — so that the comparison baseline captures rent growth during the uplift period itself. This identifies the reversal from accelerated rent growth at the uplift to decelerated growth at the re-freeze, partially bypassing both attenuation mechanisms: landlords who adjusted rents upward at the uplift do not face the same downward nominal rigidity when the floor is subsequently held fixed while market rents continue rising. R3 is therefore the better-powered specification for the fiscal capture reversal test; R1 provides a conservative lower bound. The full specification hierarchy is discussed in §5 and §6.

4. Empirical Design

4.1 Specification
The primary specification is a within-LA difference-in-differences estimator:
\[\Delta\log(\text{rent})_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta_1 (\text{lha\_intensity}_i \times \text{freeze}_t) + \mathbf{X}_{it}'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
where \(\text{freeze}_t = \mathbf{1}[t \geq \text{2021-Q3}]\), \(\alpha_i\) are LA fixed effects, \(\lambda_t\) are region-by-quarter fixed effects absorbing common shocks, and \(\mathbf{X}_{it}\) includes the quarterly unemployment rate and log 10th-percentile weekly wage. Standard errors clustered at the LA level.
The treatment variable lha_intensity is pre-period (2018–19 average), eliminating reverse-causality concerns. The freeze indicator is interacted with continuous lha_intensity rather than a binary binding indicator to exploit full intensity variation.


4.2 Two-Event Specification
The two-event specification simultaneously estimates the uplift and re-freeze effects:
\[\Delta\log(\text{rent})_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta_{\text{up}} (\text{lha\_intensity}_i \times \text{uplift}_t) + \beta_{\text{fr}} (\text{lha\_intensity}_i \times \text{freeze}_t) + \mathbf{X}_{it}'\boldsymbol{\gamma} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
where \(\text{uplift}_t = \mathbf{1}[2020\text{-Q2} \leq t \leq 2021\text{-Q2}]\) covers the 2020 restoration period and \(\text{freeze}_t = \mathbf{1}[t \geq 2021\text{-Q3}]\) is the re-freeze indicator from §4.1. Fiscal capture predicts \(\beta_{\text{up}} > 0\) (rent acceleration when the floor rises) and \(\beta_{\text{fr}} < 0\) (rent deceleration when the floor is held fixed below rising market rents). The single-event specification in §4.1 omits the uplift dummy, folding the 2020-Q2–2021-Q2 uplift quarters into the comparison baseline.


4.3 Identification Assumptions
Parallel trends: In the absence of the LHA policy events, rent growth in high-intensity and low-intensity LAs would have followed parallel trends. The R4 placebo test (\(\hat{\beta}_1\), 2015–2019, fake treatment 2018-Q1: \(p=0.562\)) supports this assumption.
Pre-treatment intensity exogeneity: lha_intensity is measured in 2018–19, before the April 2020 uplift, and is predetermined with respect to the treatment. It is also substantively interpretable (Figure 3): intensity loads strongly on local labour-market weakness — the claimant unemployment rate (\(r = 0.75\)) — while being uncorrelated with the level of local rents (\(r = 0.02\)). Exposure therefore concentrates in the areas where benefit-dependence, and hence the reproduction constraint of §7, is most acute; and because intensity is orthogonal to rent levels, the rent-growth effect cannot be an artefact of high- or low-rent areas reverting to a common trend. The design exploits variation in the benefit-dependent share of the local market, not in its price.






Figure 3: Treatment characterisation. Each point is one of 286 England local authorities. Left: LHA intensity against the mean claimant unemployment rate — exposure concentrates in the weakest labour markets (correlation 0.75). Right: LHA intensity against the mean two-bedroom rent — intensity is uncorrelated with rent levels (correlation 0.02), so the treatment is not a proxy for area rents. London boroughs are marked separately.



No anticipation: LHA re-freeze announced at Autumn Statement 2020; the 2021-Q3 indicator incorporates a one-quarter implementation lag.

5.3 The Mechanistic Isolator (R20)
R20 combines the COVID-window restriction (R3: uses the 2020-Q2 uplift period as baseline, providing the cleanest identification of the re-freeze reversal) with the density control (R15: strips urban demand recovery attenuation). The result, \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0675\) (\(p=0.0001\)), represents the density-adjusted, uplift-baseline estimate. It is a post-hoc, exploratory specification — not part of the pre-specified analysis and not the primary specification. It demonstrates the R3 result is density-robust by a wide margin.


5.4 Event-Study Dynamics
Figure 4 reports the dynamic analogue of the difference-in-differences estimate: the coefficient on lha_intensity interacted with each quarter, under the fixed-effect structure of the primary specification and normalised to the quarter before the re-freeze.2 The static \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) is the post-2021-Q3 average of this sequence.
The path is consistent with the yield-floor mechanism: once the allowance is frozen while market rents continue to rise, rent growth in high-intensity authorities decelerates relative to elsewhere. The coefficients are statistically indistinguishable from zero across the 2020 uplift and turn negative only after the re-freeze, reaching \(-0.075\) in 2022-Q1; the deceleration concentrates in the year following the freeze and then attenuates through 2023–24 as growth rates re-converge and the April 2024 re-linking is anticipated and implemented. We read the late-window recovery as the dynamic counterpart of the policy reversal rather than as evidence of a transient effect, while noting that the post-freeze window is too short to separate the two.
The pre-uplift coefficients are not flat: high-intensity authorities show slower rent growth through 2019. We read this as the imprint of the preceding freeze — LHA was held at 2015–16 cash terms from April 2016 — rather than a failure of the design, since the mechanism under test should itself have depressed rent growth in high-intensity areas during that episode. The reading bears directly on the specification hierarchy: because the 2019 baseline is itself a freeze period, the primary specification, which averages against the full pre-2021 window, compresses the measured contrast, whereas the COVID-window specification (R3), which takes the 2020 uplift as its comparison, removes the contaminated baseline and recovers a larger coefficient — the pattern the event study makes visible. We therefore do not rest the parallel-trends claim on visual flatness, which the LHA policy history renders implausible over any window spanning a prior freeze; the formal support is the R4 placebo (§4.3). The coefficients are imprecise throughout — only the 2022 quarters are individually distinguishable from zero — so the figure corroborates the sign and timing of the static estimate rather than supplying an independent test of significance.






Figure 4: Event study. Period-by-period coefficients on LHA intensity interacted with quarter dummies (local-authority and region-by-quarter fixed effects), normalised to the quarter before the 2021-Q3 re-freeze. Coefficients sit near zero across the 2020 uplift and turn negative after the re-freeze, reaching about -0.075 in 2022-Q1 before attenuating toward the April 2024 re-linking — the directional signature of fiscal capture across the policy sequence. Shaded bands mark the 2016 freeze, the 2020 uplift, and the 2021 re-freeze; the slower pre-uplift growth in high-intensity areas falls within the earlier freeze (§2.1) rather than a pre-trend violation. Coefficients are imprecise; parallel trends are supported formally by the R4 placebo (§4.3), not by visual flatness.

6. Robustness

6.1 Specification Robustness — 24-Specification Directional Sweep
Across the 24 fiscal capture specifications — varying the estimation window (Temporal), density controls and geographic clustering (Spatial), bedroom composition (Compositional), and outlier treatment and measurement (Measurement) — \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) is negative with zero sign reversals. The Appendix A table reports 28 rows; four are excluded from this directional count. R4 is the identification check (positive coefficient expected and confirmed) and R12a is a binary binding threshold (near-zero by construction — an absorption diagnostic, not a fiscal capture test). The remaining two — R8 and R9 — coincide with R1 by construction rather than as independent estimates, because their coverage criteria (drop thin-market and high-HMO local authorities) are satisfied by zero local authorities and so reproduce the primary coefficient exactly. The 24 counted specifications are distinct estimates. R2, which replaces the saturated Region×Quarter fixed effects with region-specific linear trends plus quarter fixed effects, is among the specifications that recover a nominally significant negative coefficient (\(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0231\), \(p = 0.043\)) once the heavy time-absorption of the primary is relaxed; R1 retains the more conservative absorption and remains the primary.
Figure 5 plots the full sweep. Every point estimate lies below zero, and no single analytical choice — temporal window, density control, clustering, bedroom composition, or outlier treatment — moves it across the line.






Figure 5: Specification curve. The re-freeze coefficient (LHA intensity interacted with the freeze indicator) across the 24 distinct fiscal-capture specifications, sorted by magnitude; the lower panel marks which analytical choices are active for each estimate. Every estimate is negative. R20 (the post-hoc mechanistic isolator) is shown in red and the supplementary HB-only specifications (R18, whose wide confidence intervals are clipped by the axis) in grey. Two construction-identical coverage variants (R8, R9) and the R4 placebo are omitted.



This directional consistency demonstrates the result is not an artifact of any single methodological choice. The 24 fiscal capture specifications are methodologically orthogonal (spanning four distinct classes of specification choice) but not statistically independent (all share the 290-LA cross-section and therefore share unobserved spatial error structure). We interpret the sweep as specification robustness, not as 24 independent pieces of frequentist evidence.
Statistical disclosure (FWER): The pre-specified family of 16 tests (R1–R15 plus R7) is reported for completeness. At \(\alpha/16 = 0.003125\), R3 (\(p = 0.0033\)) narrowly fails strict Bonferroni correction. We do not claim frequentist significance for any individual specification and rest the primary inference on the 24-specification directional sweep.


6.2 Conservative Sample Restriction (R7)
Excluding the top decile of net in-migration LAs (30 LAs; threshold \(\geq\) +1,703 persons/yr) yields \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0195\) (SE=0.0125, \(p=0.119\)) on 261 LAs — more negative than R1. Fiscal capture is not purely compositional; the effect operates in non-displacement areas. Under the LPN framework, displacement is the dominant mechanism in high-migration areas; R7 survival confirms the yield-floor mechanism operates independently.


6.3 Wage Control Sensitivity (R21)
Excluding p10 wages: \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0182\) vs R1 \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0174\) (\(\Delta\beta = 0.0008\), 0.5%). The fiscal capture coefficient absorbs virtually nothing from the wage control. Under the LPN framework, the 10th-percentile wage is a theoretical primitive — the outside option of the benefit-dependent tenant class — and its inclusion is axiomatic, not empirically contingent. A 0.5% coefficient shift is inconsistent with meaningful endogeneity: if p10 were absorbing the LHA policy shock as a mediator or collider, the divergence between R1 and R21 would need to be substantial relative to the main coefficient. The empirical insulation confirms that the theoretical endogeneity concern is inert at the scale of the 290-LA cross-section.


6.4 Bedroom Stability (R17)
All four bedroom categories (1–4 bed) yield \(\hat{\beta} \approx -0.016\) to \(-0.019\), sign-consistent and nearly identical in magnitude. The 2-bedroom primary specification is not cherry-picked.

7. Structural Interpretation

7.1 Two Lenses on the Same Coefficient
The standard fiscal capture account and the LPN reproduction account agree on the empirical prediction — \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\) in binding local authorities — but diverge on the mechanism, the welfare interpretation, and the policy prescription.
Lens 1 — Standard fiscal capture. Under the standard account, LHA in binding areas acts as a price floor: landlords in the housing benefit sub-market set rents at or near the maximum allowance, knowing tenants’ budgets are constrained at that level. When LHA is frozen and market rents rise, the floor progressively unbinds from below — LHA can no longer support rents at the market level — and rent growth in binding areas slows relative to non-binding areas. Welfare interpretation: LHA is distortionary; it transfers public funds from general revenues to private landlord yields rather than to tenant welfare. The DiD finding of \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\) is evidence of that distortion. Policy implication: redirect LHA funding away from cash subsidies and toward bricks-and-mortar supply investment that bypasses the capitalization channel.
Lens 2 — LPN reproduction compression. Under the LPN framework of Huato and Galindo (2026c), housing costs are not a generic consumption expenditure; they are inputs to the reproduction of labor power. The reproduction function \(N_{t+1} = Be^{\eta_t}N_t^{1-\gamma}C_t^{\gamma}\) requires that \(C_t\) be interpreted as non-housing consumption \((1 - s_t)Y_t\), where \(s_t\) is the rent share. LHA in binding areas acts as a reproduction subsidy: it maintains the non-housing consumption base \(C_t\) of benefit-dependent households at a level consistent with demographic reproduction along the balanced growth path. When LHA is frozen, the effective subsidy falls in real terms as market rents rise above the frozen level, compressing household reproduction capacity. Rent growth slows in binding areas not only because the yield floor recedes but because the demand base — household formation, driven by demographic reproduction — contracts. Welfare interpretation: LHA is necessary but insufficient. Its freeze has adverse demographic consequences in high-intensity areas. Policy implication: a reproduction-consistent rent ceiling plus reformed LHA: the ceiling reduces the rent share \(s_t\) toward the LPD-optimal minimum; reformed LHA (decoupled from market rents) supplements household consumption capacity directly.
Table 2 summarises the divergence. The two accounts make the same rent-growth prediction — which is why the coefficient alone cannot adjudicate between them — but part company on welfare interpretation, on the test that would distinguish them, and on what policy follows.

7.2 Why the Standard Account is Insufficient
The two lenses are observationally equivalent at the level of the rent-growth coefficient. The DiD finding of \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\) is consistent with both. They diverge sharply in their predictions on outcomes outside rent growth.
The standard fiscal capture story predicts only rent-level effects. It has no prediction for population growth, household formation, or landlord exit rates conditional on rent levels. The LPN account predicts all three: high-LHA-intensity local authorities should show slower household formation and population growth relative to non-binding areas after the 2021 re-freeze, independently of the rent growth deceleration. Testing these demographic predictions requires the ONS mid-year population estimates and MHCLG household formation data at the local authority level, matched to the same 290-LA panel. That test is outside the scope of this paper (see Galindo 2026a for the theoretical derivation).


7.3 The R7 Evidence Under Both Lenses
The conservative sample restriction (R7) is informative about the mechanism even without the demographic test. Excluding the top decile of net in-migration local authorities — areas where LPN displacement is the dominant mechanism — the coefficient strengthens: \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0195\) versus \(\hat{\beta} = -0.0174\) in the full sample. Under the standard account, this is unremarkable: displacement-prone and non-displacement areas should show equally strong fiscal capture if the mechanism is purely a yield floor. Under the LPN account, R7 survival means the yield-floor mechanism operates independently of displacement in low-migration areas — fiscal capture is systemic, not merely a compositional artefact of tenant turnover. R7 failure would have implied that the mechanism operates primarily through the displacement channel. We observe survival: the yield-floor mechanism is structurally embedded in the non-displacement subsample.


7.4 The Attenuation Mechanism and the Isolator Bracket
The LPN account provides a specific prediction about the attenuation of \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\) in the primary specification. Downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in are not frictions that disappear over time; they are structural features of the low-income rental market. LHA-dependent tenants face high moving costs, limited alternative supply, and weak outside options — precisely the conditions the LPN framework formalizes through the binding reproduction constraint. The COVID-window restriction (R3) partially addresses attenuation by using the 2020-Q2 to 2021-Q1 uplift period as the comparison baseline: this identifies the predicted reversal from accelerated rent growth at the uplift to decelerated growth at the re-freeze in high-intensity areas. That reversal — the precise fiscal-capture prediction when LHA functions as a binding yield floor that is first raised and then held fixed — is what R3 estimates, and it yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0498\) (\(p = 0.0033\)).
Two attenuators can be separated, and each was identified as a confound on theoretical grounds rather than chosen for effect. The reversal window (R3) addresses the nominal rigidity just described; a density \(\times\) freeze interaction (R15) addresses the post-COVID recovery of urban demand, which lifted rents in lower-density areas and so masked capture. Crossing the two gives Table 3.

We read this as a bracket, not a point estimate. The lower bound, \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0174\), is the incidence tenants actually experience — frictions included — and is the policy-relevant magnitude; the upper reach, \(-0.0675\), is the mechanism’s force once both confounds are netted out. That two pre-identified attenuators move the estimate the same way and partly compound is a dose-response in confound-removal: specification-searching selects one significant estimate from a scatter, whereas a coherent gradient that emerges as named confounds are removed is not easily manufactured.
The bracket also marks where the two accounts part company on what the effect is. The standard reading treats \(-0.0675\) as the underlying parameter and \(-0.0174\) as friction-attenuated noise to be cleaned away. Under LPN the frictions are not measurement nuisance: downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in are the structural condition of the benefit-dependent class. The lived \(-0.0174\) is then not a biased-down estimate of a frictionless truth but the genuine short-run incidence under the actual structure — and because lock-in erodes as tenants are eventually forced to move or renegotiate, realised capture migrates from the lower bound toward the upper reach the longer the freeze runs. That migration is the mechanism behind the continuously declining effective transfer documented in §7.5 and §9. R20, which combines both adjustments, remains post-hoc and corroborating rather than primary (§8).


7.5 Implications for Fiscal Policy Evaluation
The standard framework for evaluating housing benefit in the UK public finance literature asks whether LHA expenditure achieves its stated purpose of sustaining housing access for low-income households. The fiscal capture evidence implies a partial negative answer: a substantial share of the transfer is absorbed in higher rents rather than retained in tenant welfare, so the benefit is diluted in transmission. From this vantage point, the appropriate fiscal policy response is benefit redesign — tighter caps, direct payment reform, or supply-side investment that bypasses the capitalization channel.
The LPN account identifies a deeper difficulty with this framing. If LHA functions as a reproduction subsidy — maintaining the non-housing consumption base of benefit-dependent households at a level consistent with demographic reproduction — then evaluating it as a rent-payment mechanism misidentifies its structural role. A benefit-incidence calculation finding 60–67% landlord capture (Gibbons and Manning 2006) implies not only that tenants receive roughly 33–40 pence per pound of LHA; it implies that the reproduction subsidy is 60–67% ineffective in sustaining the consumption base it is designed to protect, and that this effective subsidy rate has been declining in real terms throughout the 2021–24 re-freeze as market rents rose above the frozen allowance. The fiscal policy question is not only how much of the transfer is capitalized, but how much reproduction capacity is sustained per pound of LHA expenditure, and the answer to the latter has been deteriorating continuously since 2021.
This reframing shifts the appropriate metric for fiscal evaluation. If the policy goal is reproduction-capacity maintenance rather than rent-payment sufficiency, the relevant benchmark is not whether LHA covers the 30th percentile of local market rents — a distribution that is itself partly inflated by prior capitalization cycles — but whether LHA, net of landlord capture, sustains the non-housing consumption floor for benefit-dependent households at or above the reproduction-consistent minimum. LHA policy that periodically re-links to the 30th percentile does not reduce the rent share; it resets the baseline for the next capitalization cycle. The April 2024 re-linking and the April 2025 re-freeze confirm this cycle is structurally embedded in the current design (Bangham et al. 2026). Both theoretical lenses reach the same negative verdict: LHA reform cannot be assessed solely on its rate-setting rules. The standard account demands assessment on the incidence-adjusted net transfer to tenant welfare; the LPN account extends this to the net transfer to tenant reproduction capacity. On both metrics, a benefit that is periodically uplifted only to be immediately re-frozen provides no durable improvement.

text:
8. Limitations

Statistical power: The primary specification is underpowered. A 12-quarter post-freeze window is short relative to the adjustment horizon; downward nominal rigidity further attenuates \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}}\). R3 (COVID-window) and R20 (R3+density) provide better-powered estimates.
Post-2021 austerity confound: General fiscal tightening in high-deprivation local authorities after 2021 is correlated with lha_intensity through the deprivation channel. If austerity reduced housing demand in high-intensity areas, it could produce \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} < 0\) through a demand channel unrelated to the LHA yield floor. Three pieces of evidence run against this confounder. First, the COVID-window restriction (R3: 2020-Q2–2024-Q1) uses the 2020 fiscal-stimulus period as the comparison baseline; under the austerity hypothesis, R3 should be weaker than R1 (because the comparison window includes peak stimulus). Instead R3 (\(\hat{\beta} = -0.0498\)) is nearly three times larger than R1 (\(\hat{\beta} = -0.0174\)), consistent with the uplift-to-re-freeze reversal mechanism rather than with an austerity demand channel. Second, the R4 placebo (2015–2019, covering the initial 2016 freeze and significant austerity) yields \(\hat{\beta} = +0.0085\) (\(p = 0.562\)): high-intensity areas show no negative rent growth in the first austerity wave, which would not be expected if deprivation-correlated demand compression were the mechanism. Third, Region×Quarter fixed effects absorb common regional fiscal shocks; residual within-region lha_intensity variation would need to be driven by LA-specific austerity heterogeneity beyond regional trends to confound the estimate. Fourth, pre-period LHA intensity is orthogonal to local rent levels (\(r = 0.02\); Figure 3), so the treatment is not a proxy for area rent fundamentals — the channel through which a generic local-demand or supply-inelasticity story would have to operate. A full rebuttal of the austerity channel specifically would require quarterly LA-level public expenditure data, which remains a limitation of this analysis.
R20 post-hoc status: The mechanistic isolator (R20) is post-hoc rather than pre-specified. It is corroborating, not primary.
p10 wage endogeneity: ASHE annual frequency precludes formal empirical resolution of the collider question. The R21 sensitivity (§6.3) provides partial empirical insulation: the 0.5% coefficient shift when p10 is excluded is inconsistent with meaningful mediation or over-absorption of the LHA treatment shock. PAYE RTI (monthly) remains the preferred upgrade for formal resolution.

title: Fiscal Capture in the UK PRS
text:
9. Conclusion
The UK Local Housing Allowance provides a rare natural experiment for identifying fiscal capture: two policy events with directionally opposite predictions in a difference-in-differences framework that uses pre-period intensity variation across 290 local authorities. The empirical pattern is consistent with the fiscal capture prediction across every combination of estimation window, spatial control, bedroom composition, and outlier treatment we examine. The directional signature — decelerated rent growth in binding areas at the re-freeze, consistent with the predicted reversal from the uplift baseline — holds in 24 fiscal capture specifications with zero sign reversals.
The primary specification is underpowered by construction. Downward nominal rigidity and tenant lock-in attenuate the re-freeze coefficient exactly when fiscal capture is real, so \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0174\) (\(p = 0.142\)) is best interpreted as a lower bound on the underlying effect. The COVID-window restriction, which identifies the directional reversal more sharply, yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0498\) (\(p = 0.0033\)). After additionally stripping post-COVID urban demand recovery attenuation via a density interaction, the mechanistic isolator yields \(\hat{\beta}_{\text{fr}} = -0.0675\) (\(p = 0.0001\)). The conservative sample restriction excluding high net in-migration local authorities produces a more negative coefficient than the full-sample estimate, confirming that fiscal capture is not purely compositional: the yield-floor mechanism operates in areas without significant displacement pressure.
These results are consistent with both the standard fiscal capture account and the LPN reproduction account. The two accounts are observationally equivalent at the level of rent-growth coefficients; they diverge on whether LHA is distortionary (standard account) or structurally necessary (LPN account). The distinguishing empirical test — whether binding local authorities show slower household formation and population growth relative to non-binding areas after the 2021 re-freeze — is outside the scope of this paper and is the subject of ongoing work.
For policy, the results confirm that the 2021–24 LHA re-freeze progressively reduced the effective transfer to benefit-dependent households: as market rents rose above the frozen allowance, the share of LHA retained in tenant welfare — rather than capitalized by landlords — declined continuously. Under the LPN account, this constitutes erosion of the reproduction subsidy that LHA provides to benefit-dependent households in the private rented sector. The April 2024 re-linking, itself frozen again in April 2025, has merely reset the cycle. Under either theoretical lens — fiscal capture or reproduction compression — LHA policy that bounces between temporary uplifts and persistent freezes is structurally inadequate (Bangham et al. 2026). The LPN account implies the additional prescription: a reproduction-consistent rent ceiling that reduces the rent share toward the LPD-optimal minimum (characterized formally in Huato and Galindo 2026c), not merely a periodic re-linking of the benefit rate to an already overinflated market rent distribution.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
text: Carlos Galindo Escajeda June 3, 2026

title: A Progressing Problemshift
text:
Abstract
The economic case for rent regulation that NEF increasingly draws on rests on a body of heterodox theory — a four-paper research programme arguing that Britain’s rented sector is a financialised asset class in which the textbook objection to rent control does not apply. Intellectual armour of that kind is only as good as its rigour. This paper asks, in the mainstream philosophy of science’s own terms, whether the programme behind those policy arguments is sound — and answers with deliberate, defensible restraint rather than advocacy.
Using the appraisal framework orthodox economists themselves respect — Imre Lakatos’s methodology of scientific research programmes — it reconstructs the four papers as a single programme: one declared foundation (the reproduction of labour power as the measure of value, in place of the standard efficiency criterion), a protective belt of four falsifiable applications, and one method — turning orthodox economics’ own mathematical apparatus against its conclusions. It then asks the question Lakatos’s framework was built to answer: is the programme progressing?
The verdict is split, and candid about it. The programme is theoretically progressive — under criticism it has replaced free assumptions with tighter, testable restrictions — and non-degenerating: challenged repeatedly, it narrowed its claims rather than inflating them. But the decisive empirical test that would distinguish it from the orthodox account is named, designed, and not yet run. The programme is progressing; it is not yet proven progressive, and it says so.
For NEF the relevance is direct. The economics it cites in defence of rent regulation is not rhetoric but a programme built to be checked, transparent about exactly where its evidence stops. Work that states its own limits this precisely is the kind that withstands hostile scrutiny in policy debate — and that standard is one this reconstruction both describes and is itself held to.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
section: 1. Introduction — a programme, and the question of appraisal
text:
1. Introduction — a programme, and the question of appraisal
Heterodox research in economics is routinely refused appraisal rather than refuted. Its premises are declared inadmissible at the threshold — too political, too unorthodox in their primitives, insufficiently neutral — and the question of whether a given body of heterodox work is internally progressive or degenerating is never reached.1 This paper takes one recent body of such work and insists on reaching that question.
The object is a four-paper sequence. A theory paper takes the reproduction of labour power, rather than subjective utility, as the primitive in which value is reckoned, and replaces Pareto efficiency with a criterion it calls Labor-Power Dominance. A structural paper derives, from that criterion, a reproduction-consistent ceiling on rent. An empirical paper studies the capitalisation of a housing subsidy into rents. A policy paper argues that the orthodox objection to rent regulation is inapplicable to the financialised market that actually exists. The four are not four arguments; they are one argument distributed across four artifacts.
The appraisal question worth asking is not “is the programme true?” Lakatos’s central methodological move was to separate the truth of a research programme from its progressivity — whether, over time, it generates excess content and meets criticism by adding to its explanatory reach rather than by patching anomalies [Lakatos 1970]. A programme’s hard core, on this account, is held immune by the methodological decision of its practitioners; the core is not what gets tested. What gets tested is the protective belt, and the appraisal verdict turns on how the belt is revised under pressure. This paper addresses only that verdict. It is the central discipline of what follows that we never convert the appraisal into an endorsement of the core: showing that a programme develops progressively is not showing that its founding commitment is correct, and the two must not be allowed to bleed into one another.
The contribution is threefold and modest. First, a rational reconstruction of a heterodox economics programme in explicit Lakatosian terms — uncommon in itself. Second, a reconstruction that is checkable: the programme was developed under a recorded sequence of adversarial review, so the claim “the belt was revised progressively while the core stayed fixed” can be audited against a contemporaneous construction record rather than rested on retrospective narrative. Third, and most important methodologically, a reconstruction that performs the discipline it describes — including by demoting the programme’s own most rhetorically convenient result when that result does not, in fact, discriminate the programme from its rival.
What this paper is not: it is not a defence of the truth of labour-power-as-numéraire or of Labor-Power Dominance; it is not a claim that the programme’s policy conclusions are correct; and it is not a new criterion of demarcation. Section 2 sets out the Lakatosian apparatus and justifies its selection. Sections 3–5 identify the hard core, the four-ply belt, and the positive heuristic. Section 6 delivers the split appraisal. Section 7 treats the construction record as bounded corroboration. Section 8 states the limits, including the conflict of interest inherent in reconstructing one’s own programme. Section 9 concludes.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
text:
2. The Lakatosian apparatus (imported, not defended)
Lakatos’s methodology of scientific research programmes distinguishes a hard core of central commitments, held immune from refutation by the practitioners’ methodological decision; a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that bear the brunt of testing and are revised when anomalies arise; and a positive heuristic that directs how the belt is to be developed [Lakatos 1970]. The unit of appraisal is the programme over time, not the individual paper or the isolated test.
The crucial feature for what follows is that the core is held immune by decision. This is not a claim that the core is unfalsifiable in principle, nor a licence to believe it; it is a description of how programmes actually allocate the risk of refutation — anomalies are charged to the belt, and the core is protected so long as the practitioners choose to protect it. That choice is itself revisable: practitioners of a degenerating programme do, eventually, abandon their cores. Immunity, then, is a methodological stance, not a dogma, and a programme earns no credit merely for holding a core fixed. It earns credit only if the core is held fixed while the belt does progressive work — and, as Section 6.2 insists, only if the core was genuinely attacked and nonetheless preserved without ad hoc rescue.
Lakatos’s appraisal criterion is comparative and historical. A problemshift is theoretically progressive if each modification of the belt predicts some novel fact the predecessor did not; it is empirically progressive if some of that excess content is corroborated; and it is degenerating if the belt is revised only to accommodate known anomalies, generating no new testable content [Lakatos 1970]. These are graded, not binary, and they are judged over a development sequence — which is precisely what a documented construction history supplies.
Why Lakatos here, and not Kuhn or Laudan? Kuhn’s apparatus of paradigms and normal science lacks a fine-grained, within-programme criterion for distinguishing progress from degeneration; it describes the sociology of theory change better than it adjudicates it [Kuhn 1962]. Laudan’s problem-solving model offers an appraisal criterion, but one keyed to a programme’s net problem-solving effectiveness across empirical and conceptual problems — harder to operationalise from a textual record, and less naturally mapped onto a programme with a single declared normative primitive [Laudan 1977]. Lakatos’s core/belt architecture maps directly onto a multi-paper programme built around one ontological commitment with a logged development history. The choice is a scoping decision, defended as such; it is not a claim that Lakatos’s framework is the uniquely correct philosophy of science, and Section 8 records the meta-objection that the framework itself may be ill-suited to economics.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
section: 3. The hard core — identified, and (by design) not defended
text:
3. The hard core — identified, and (by design) not defended
The programme has a single, stable hard core, and it is stated as such in the theory paper: value is reckoned in the reproduction of living labour power, and social states are ranked by a criterion of Labor-Power Dominance that replaces Pareto efficiency rather than refining it. The theory paper is explicit that this is a change of primitive — “the materialist primitive is society’s reproductive capacity — not subjective utility” — and that the resulting criterion is incommensurable with the Paretian one: Labor-Power Dominance “is structurally linear (risk-neutral) in expected” labour power and “can rank an allocation as dominant that a Paretian welfare function would reject, and vice versa.” The core is, in short, declared — held out as a chosen primitive, not presented as a neutral default.
This paper does not defend that choice, and the refusal is principled, not evasive. Within the Lakatosian framework a hard core is held immune by the programme’s methodological decision; it is not the object of test. To demand that the programme empirically prove labour-power-as-numéraire before its development can be appraised is to misunderstand the unit of appraisal — it is to charge to the core a burden the framework assigns to the belt. We therefore claim only two things about the core, both of which are checkable and neither of which is a truth-claim: that it is declared, and that it was kept fixed across the development. The second claim is load-bearing and is established in Section 6.2, where it is shown that the core was kept fixed not by default but under direct and recorded attack.
A clarification forestalls the obvious objection that immunity is a dogmatic cheat. Immunity is a revisable decision (Section 2): a programme whose core must be rescued ever more elaborately is free to abandon it, and degenerating programmes do. The asymmetry we will draw with orthodoxy in Section 8 is therefore not that this programme has a normative core while orthodoxy does not — every welfare economics fixes a numéraire, which is the foundational normative act — but that this programme declares its core as a choice, whereas the competitive-efficiency benchmark typically operates as an undeclared default. We rest no part of the appraisal on that asymmetry; we note it.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
section: 4. The protective belt — four papers, four plies
text:
4. The protective belt — four papers, four plies
The four papers are best read not as four programmes, nor as four independent applications, but as one protective belt of four plies around the Section 3 core. The claim that they form a single belt rather than parallel exercises rests on two observable features, and intellectual honesty requires stating the second one precisely rather than asserting a tidier unity than the texts support.
First, the four share the core ontology: each takes the reproduction of labour power, not utility, as the primitive against which its object is evaluated. Second, three of them are wired into one explicit citation-dependency structure, with a documented asymmetry for the fourth. The theory paper (2026c) is the hub: the structural paper sources its reproduction function, its stochastic-discount factor, and its maintained assumptions to it, and the empirical paper rests its structural interpretation on it. The structural paper (2026a) and the empirical paper (2026b) are reciprocally wired: the structural paper defers its empirics to the empirical paper, and the empirical paper defers its theoretical derivation back to the structural paper. The policy paper is the exception that must be conceded: it cites none of the other three, and is cited inward by the structural paper (for its supply-inelasticity diagnosis and its treatment of the policy instrument) without citing back. The policy ply therefore belongs to the belt by shared ontology and inward citation only, not by an outward citation of its own — a looser coupling than the theory–structural–empirical triangle, and we do not pretend otherwise. The unit that develops over time is nonetheless the programme: the hub-and-triangle citation structure plus the shared primitive is what makes the four plies one belt rather than four parallel exercises, even with the policy ply attached at one edge rather than woven through.

Ply 1 — the value theory. A materialist macro-finance model in which the reproduction of labour power is the primitive, the stochastic discount factor is derived from the Bellman multipliers on reproductive capacity rather than posited, and a closed-form materialist risk premium is obtained (Theorem 4.1, discussed in Section 6). This ply supplies the formal core and the welfare criterion.
Ply 2 — the structural derivation. From the dominance criterion, a reproduction-consistent rent ceiling is derived, conditional on a maintained empirical premise that the housing asset is overvalued relative to its reproduction-consistent price. The conditionality is stated in the paper, not concealed.
Ply 3 — the empirical identification. A difference-in-differences study of the capitalisation of a housing subsidy into rents, reporting robust directional results across many specifications.
Ply 4 — the policy defence. An argument that, in a market whose competitive preconditions are demonstrably absent, the orthodox second-best objection to rent regulation is inapplicable — and, symmetrically, that deregulation enjoys no first-best presumption either.

The plies exhibit what may be called four honesties: each declares a specific non-result at the exact point where overclaiming would be most tempting. The structural ply declares its overvaluation premise a maintained premise. The empirical ply reports its headline coefficient as a lower bound and concedes an observational equivalence its data cannot break. The policy ply holds its central theorem to its strictly negative form, claiming non-exclusion rather than optimality. The theory ply distinguishes what it proves (a conditional risk-premium theorem) from what it defers (the criterion’s full axiomatics). These honesties are not modesty for its own sake; Section 6 shows they are the evidence of non-degeneration, and must be kept rigorously distinct from the evidence of content-increase, with which a careless reading would conflate them.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
section: 5. The positive heuristic — immanent critique with borrowed engines
text:
5. The positive heuristic — immanent critique with borrowed engines
The belt is not developed opportunistically. It is developed by a single rule: take an instrument the orthodox tradition trusts, and turn it on the tradition’s own conclusion. This is immanent critique in the strict sense — not an external denunciation of the mainstream from foreign premises, but an internal demonstration that the mainstream’s own apparatus, applied to its own object, yields a conclusion the mainstream disfavours. The theory paper states the strategy without euphemism: it pursues “deliberate methodological immanence,” in which “the same Bellman apparatus that standard macro deploys to establish the efficiency of competitive institutions is here turned to demonstrate that those institutions generate structurally necessary violations of the materialist welfare criterion.” Competitive institutions, in the model, “do not fail … by failing to solve their own Paretian optimization problem but by solving it perfectly.”
The heuristic is instantiated four times with four borrowed engines:2 the asset-pricing / perturbation apparatus in the theory ply; the planner’s constrained-optimisation problem in the structural ply; the difference-in-differences design — the workhorse of orthodox programme evaluation — in the empirical ply; and the general theory of the second best together with the Diamond–Mirrlees production-efficiency result in the policy ply. That the heuristic is rule-governed in this way is itself an appraisal-relevant fact: a programme whose belt grows by a stated heuristic is one whose growth can be assessed for excess content, rather than dismissed as post-hoc fitting.
A standing objection must be registered: does adopting the rival’s apparatus concede the rival’s frame? The programme’s answer is that the indictment targets the institutions the apparatus certifies, not the apparatus’s internal logic — and that inhabiting the frame is precisely what makes the verdict binding rather than question-begging. We report this as the programme’s heuristic and as the source of its dialectical reach; we do not here advance it as a universal method, an ambition Section 8 records as deferred.

title: A Progressing Problemshift
section: 6. The appraisal — theoretically progressive, non-degenerating, empirically progressing
text:
6. The appraisal — theoretically progressive, non-degenerating, empirically progressing
We now apply Lakatos’s graded criterion. The verdict is deliberately split into three, because the artifacts support the three components to different degrees, and collapsing them into a single “the programme is progressive” would be the precise auto-goal this paper exists to avoid.

6.1 Theoretical progressivity: a content-increasing development step
The decisive question under Lakatos is not whether the programme possesses a sharp result — a sharp result shows only that its content is high, not that its development was progressive — but whether a revision of the belt added content under pressure. The programme furnishes one clean, documented instance, and it is best presented as a development step rather than as a founding endowment.
In an earlier state, the theory ply contained only a conjecture about the demographic component of the risk premium: the second covariance term was identified but its coefficient was unproven and its derivation explicitly deferred. Under subsequent review the conjecture was discharged into a conditional theorem (Theorem 4.1) with a closed-form coefficient and a signed result. The materialist risk premium takes the form \[
\mathbb{E}_t[R_{K,t+1}] - R_{f,t} \approx \sigma\gamma\,\operatorname{Cov}_t(\Delta\tilde{c}_{t+1}, R_{K,t+1})
+ (1-\gamma)\,\Omega\,\operatorname{Cov}_t(\Delta n_{t+2}, R_{K,t+1}),
\] with the demographic-risk coefficient pinned in closed form, \[
(1-\gamma)\,\Omega \;=\; -\,\frac{\psi_x\,\xi_\theta}{\gamma\,\varphi_\theta},
\] where \(\psi_x\) is a Bellman curvature elasticity, \(\xi_\theta\) the net capital-ratio savings response, \(\varphi_\theta\) the consumption response, and \(\gamma\) the reproduction elasticity.
What makes this a content-increasing step, and not an ad hoc rescue, is that the revision removed degrees of freedom. Standard consumption-CAPM can match any observed risk premium by freely calibrating the risk-aversion parameter. The revised belt binds the effective risk price to physical reproduction-technology parameters: the modeller is no longer free to choose it.3 A revision that converts a free parameter into a constrained, in-principle-testable function of named primitives is the structural opposite of a degenerating manoeuvre, which would instead add free parameters to absorb an anomaly. The exhibit, properly stated, is the transition from conjecture to signed theorem; the static theorem alone would not establish progressivity, only high content.
Two clarifications pre-empt predictable objections. First, this is an appraisal of a logical relation between two public states of an artifact — an earlier draft in which the coefficient was an unproven conjecture, and a later one in which it is a signed closed-form restriction — not a claim about the authors’ psychology or the wall-clock interval between them. In Popper’s terms the relation lives in World 3 (the objective content of the theories), not World 2 (the private process of authoring); that the transition happened quickly, or within a short span of one programme’s development, neither establishes nor undermines it. The objection “this is mere intra-draft editing” is therefore a category error: editing is a World-2 activity, content-increase is a World-3 property, and the second is read off the two artifact-states regardless of how the first proceeded. Second, the restriction is not merely tidier; it forbids more. The conjecture permitted any value of the demographic risk loading; the theorem ties it, by a cross-equation identity, to independently estimable elasticities (\(\psi_x,\xi_\theta,\varphi_\theta,\gamma\)), so that ranges of jointly-estimated values which the conjecture allowed are now ruled out. Excess testable content, in the precise Popperian sense of saying more by forbidding more, is exactly what this delivers — whether or not the forbidding has yet been put to data (Section 6.3).
One scope limit must be stated plainly, on pain of the auto-goal this paper exists to avoid. A single content-increasing step (with one reinforcing internal exhibit) shows that the programme has begun a progressive problemshift; it does not show a track record of repeated such steps, which is what a mature programme accumulates. This is why the paper claims, in its title and throughout, a progressing problemshift — an indefinite article doing deliberate work — and not an established progressive programme. The verdict is “progression underway and non-degenerating,” not “progressivity proven over a development series.”
A second, purely internal exhibit reinforces the point: in the structural ply, a value-flow separability assumption converts an ambiguous interior optimum into a corner solution that fixes the policy parameter — replacing an indeterminate object with a falsifiable one under explicitly stated maintained assumptions. Again, determinacy increases and modelling freedom decreases.
It must be stated precisely what this does and does not show. The restriction’s excess content over the orthodox rival (consumption-CAPM cannot generate such a cross-equation tie) discharges the heuristic obligation of Section 5. Its status as a conjecture-to-theorem transition discharges the progressivity obligation of this section. These are two distinct claims about the same artifact and are kept separate; neither is a claim that the restriction is empirically corroborated, which is the subject of Section 6.3.


6.2 Non-degeneration: the core was attacked, not merely kept
A programme is degenerating if it saves its core by proliferating untestable auxiliaries. This programme did the opposite on two counts.
First, under attack the belt restricted its own claims rather than inflating them. The empirical coefficient was declared a lower bound; the structural overvaluation claim was narrowed to a maintained premise with explicit scope; an observational equivalence was conceded; the policy theorem was held to its negative form. These are retreats, not content-increases, and it would be an auto-goal to count them as progress. Their correct Lakatosian role is different and specific: they show that when the programme met resistance, it responded by honestly restricting scope, not by manufacturing auxiliary hypotheses to rescue an overclaim. That is the signature of non-degeneration.
Second — and this is what converts “the core was kept fixed” from a triviality into evidence — the core was genuinely attacked and survived without mutation. The construction record and cross-draft comparison document recurrent, direct assaults on the core itself: objections pressing the programme to collapse its dominance criterion back into a Paretian or utilitarian one (recorded variously as the “dual-welfare schism” objection, the “unify-the-planner” demand, and the “schizophrenic planner” objection — each, in effect, an argument that the programme cannot maintain a non-Paretian welfare primitive).4 Each was met by belt revision or by principled refusal — for instance, by showing that the demanded price–quantity duality holds only for a utilitarian objective, which the programme has declined to adopt — and in no case by altering the core. A core that survives sustained attempts to overturn it is preserved under pressure; a core never challenged would be merely retained. The evidence supports the former.


6.3 Empirical status: corroborated shared content, and the discriminating frontier
This is the sharpest point in the appraisal, and the one most exposed to an auto-goal. The empirical ply corroborates the programme’s directional prediction (the sign of the fiscal-capture effect) and sharpened its identification under criticism, through a COVID-window restriction and a density-controlled specification. Two demotions are mandatory.
First, sharper identification of an existing claim is better testing, not excess content; it strengthens confidence in a prediction the programme already made, rather than corroborating a new one. Second, and decisively: the corroborated directional fact is, in the empirical paper’s own words, “observationally equivalent at the level of the rent-growth coefficient”5 between the programme’s account and the orthodox fiscal-incidence account. A fact that both the programme and its rival predict is shared content, not the rival-beating novel content Lakatos’s empirical progressivity requires. Corroborating it confirms the programme is not refuted on shared ground; it buys the programme nothing over orthodoxy. To present this corroboration as empirical progressivity would be exactly the move the no-auto-goal discipline forbids, and the empirical paper itself is the source that forbids it.
Where, then, is the programme’s discriminating content? In precisely what is not yet corroborated: the cross-equation restriction of Section 6.1, which makes a prediction consumption-CAPM cannot, and the deferred demographic predictions (differential household formation and population dynamics) that the empirical paper names as the test that would separate the two accounts and explicitly places outside its own scope. This is the programme’s live frontier. Its status is a conjecture awaiting test, and we label it as such.
Hence the bounded verdict: the programme is theoretically progressive (6.1) and non-degenerating (6.2); its empirical development to date corroborates shared content and sharpens identification, but its rival-beating empirical progressivity is pending, contingent on a registered, falsifiable test. The programme is progressing — its excess content is theoretical and its discriminating empirical test is specified but unrun — which is a defensible Lakatosian status, and a different and weaker claim than “empirically progressive.” A theoretically progressive programme with discriminating corroboration outstanding is permitted by Lakatos and is not degenerating; it is a candidate whose empirical verdict is open.
Two clarifications keep this verdict honest. First, on Lakatos’s own account empirical corroboration need not be instantaneous for theoretical progressivity to be credited: a programme remains theoretically progressive so long as its heuristic keeps generating novel, testable, degrees-of-freedom-reducing content, even while the apparatus to test that content is still being built (Lakatos 1970). We report the frontier not as a failure of progress but as the precise condition of a theoretically progressive programme whose discriminating predictions are now well-posed for the next empirical step. Second, the observational equivalence does not make the two accounts theoretically equivalent, and Occam’s razor does not favour the rival: the orthodox fiscal-incidence model is not simpler, it is narrower — it predicts the rent-growth coefficient but is structurally silent on demographic reproduction paths and on the cross-equation restriction that pins the effective risk price to physical parameters. Silence on those dimensions is not equivalence. The programme generates additional excess theoretical content the rival cannot produce. This is a wider untested falsifiable frontier, not a superiority verdict: because that excess content is as yet uncorroborated, it does not (and on the no-auto-goal discipline must not) establish that the programme beats its rival — only that it is not redundant with it.
A symmetric possibility must be granted, because it follows from the same logic and a careful reader will raise it: orthodoxy might simply annex the cross-equation restriction — treat the demographic risk loading as an interesting friction bolted onto an otherwise unchanged consumption-CAPM — while discarding the materialist core that motivated it. This would be no embarrassment to the present claim, and it is worth seeing why. If the restriction is adopted and corroborated, that is the excess content vindicated as content the rival previously lacked, which is Lakatosian progress for the content. What annexation would threaten is the programme’s distinctness — its standing as a separate programme rather than a tributary feeding the mainstream — not its progressivity. Those are different appraisals, and this paper makes only the second. That the programme’s most testable contribution is also the one most liable to absorption by its rival is a fact about its porous boundary, recorded here, not a defect in the progressivity verdict.
